speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had intended at this time to make a statement on the critical events in Cyprus during the past few days. subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR FLOUR MILL EMPLOYEES, SASKATOON
ASSISTANCE FOR FLOUR MILL EMPLOYEES, SASKATOON
speechtext:
1.	Has the Minister of Trade and Commerce received a letter from the united packing house workers of America, district 10 of Saskatoon, expressing their vital concern that every effort be made toward negotiating contracts providing that a proportion of the export wheat sold on long term credit be milled flour?
2.	What steps can the minister announce which will help alleviate the problem facing flour mill employees in Saskatoon?

Orders for Returns

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR FLOUR MILL EMPLOYEES, SASKATOON
speechtext:
1. Yes, I have received the letter referred to, and I have already replied to it.
2. Competition for wheat markets is extremely keen and under these conditions it would not be appropriate for Canada to attempt to force a country to purchase flour instead of wheat just because credit facilities had been extended. Most of these countries already have adequate milling facilities of their own.
There have been many countries in recent years, former customers for Canada's flour, who have undertaken the construction of their own mills. There is nothing that Canada can do to halt this trend, except to ensure that our wheat finds a market in such countries, and this we are doing. Such construction has, however, reduced the level of Canadian flour exports and intensified world competition for remaining flour markets.
The government and the officials of my department take every opportunity to draw to the attention of potential foreign buyers the quality and character of Canadian flour. In the recent long term agreements signed with the U.S.S.R., Bulgaria and Hungary, during the 1963-64 crop year, buyers agreed to the option of taking wheat over the next three years in the form of grain, or in the form of flour.
As reported in the house on Tuesday, July 28, (see Hansard page 6063) I had a delegation from the millers association meet with me in my office to review the outlook for the industry and examine the possibility of providing flour to underdeveloped countries through foreign aid. It is, however, not likely that there will be foreign orders for flour of the same magnitude as last year. Nevertheless, the government continues to extend a maximum effort to increase flour sales abroad.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as indicated by my hon. friend the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and without going into any arguments at this moment, I wish to make a motion seconded by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr).
I ask leave to move the adjournment of this house under the provisions of standing order 26 in order to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the most recent turn of events in Cyprus which seriously threatens the peace of the world and gravely endangers the solidarity of the NATO alliance, and also places in a critical situation our Canadian contingent with the United Nations peace keeping force in Cyprus because of the vagueness of the terms of reference for that force and the lack of the authority necessary for it to act effectively.
Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister) r
Mr. Speaker, the government desires to support this motion, which deals with a matter of extreme importance and, indeed, urgency. Because of the delicacy and indeed the dangers of the situation alluded to by my right hon. friend, I know that all hon. members will wish to deal with the question with a special sense of responsibility. This applies particularly, of course, to the spokesmen for the government, who will be bound on this occasion not only by the limits of security but will also say nothing, as I am sure all hon. members would wish, which would prejudice the success of the United Nations operations or the very delicate negotiations which are now going on at the United Nations.

speechtext:

In my opinion this meets all the requirements of standing order No. 26 with regard to the urgency of debate. I therefore put the motion as follows:

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated on motions I propose to take advantage of the initiative of my right hon. friend to make a report to the house in connection with the critical events which began on Friday last on Cyprus.
The situation in Cyprus began to deteriorate rapidly on August 6 apparently as the result of a Greek Cypriot drive to close off the access to the sea and reinforcements from
Cyprus Crisis
Turkey for the Turkish-Cypriot community in the Mansoura-Kokkina area of northwest Cyprus. Incidentally, in that area Canadian UN troops have not participated. They are located in another area. In this particular instance the contingent of Sweden played a notable part.
As has been the case now for some months, and of course since the most recent developments, the government has been in close touch with events in Cyprus, with developments at the United Nations, with the action taken by the NATO council, with developments in Ankara and Athens and, of course, particularly with our United States and United Kingdom friends.
The Canadian high commissioner in Nicosia has reported fully on the events as they took place in Cyprus, and I am in receipt of a report from him as of two hours ago. I may say that he has been in constant touch with the government of Cyprus during these and other days.
On August 9 a message was delivered to Archbishop Makarios from the Prime Minister of Canada expressing concern at the developments which were taking place, and urging that the fighting on the island cease and that use be made of the United Nations forces to supervise a cease fire.
We are also, of course, in close touch with the United Nations authorities in respect of the Canadian force on the island. My colleague the Minister of National Defence has taken all necessary steps, as he announced yesterday, to ensure that the Canadian troops are prepared for any contingency; but, as he said, any decision in that regard is one that rests with the United Nations. Action with respect to the deployment of our troops would, of course, follow decisions by the United Nations.
Our ambassador in that body has been in close contact with the secretary general himself and with senior United Nations officials, and I spoke this morning by telephone with the secretary general. The security council met on the night of August 8 and later passed a resolution, the text of which I should like to table now, appealing for a cease fire. A further meeting of the security council was called for today at the instance of two of the parties, but 1 understand the government of Greece has withdrawn its application for this meeting. It is not now probable that a meeting will take place today. A further meeting of the security council may possibly take place tomorrow.

Cyprus Crisis
I attach the greatest importance to the effectiveness of action by the security council, bringing to bear as it does the pressure of world opinion in favour of immediate action to prevent further violence on Cyprus. I am sure the house will share with me the view that if it were not for the fact that the security council met and that there was a United Nations which made such action possible, the events of the last two days might not have taken the more favourable turn that has since developed.
Naturally I have likewise been in touch with members of the NATO council, because two of the countries involved are members of the alliance. Yesterday the Prime Minister telephoned the President of the United States and he later had a further call on behalf of the President from the secretary of state. I myself had a conversation later in the afternoon with Mr. Rusk.
The Canadian charge d'affaires in Athens was received by the foreign minister of Greece on August 9, and here in Ottawa I asked the ambassador for Greece and the Turkish charge d'affaires to come and see me. I made known to them Canadian views with regard to this situation and asked both of them to urge on their governments the need to take every precaution to avoid a continuation of the hostilities that had begun. Although I had sent a message to the foreign ministers of Greece and Turkey, 1 thought it well to supplement this by conversations with the heads of their missions in Ottawa.
Also on Friday I addressed a message to the foreign minister of Turkey asking him in the name of the government of Canada to take every step to cause a cessation of hostilities, and particularly to hold back the air force operations of his government. I added to that a call yesterday directly to Ankara to Mr. Erkin, the foreign minister, explaining our concern at the way in which the situation was developing.
Throughout this crisis we have, of course, been in constant touch with the United States and the United Kingdom as well as the authorities of other governments. On a number of occasions we have been in close consultation with the state department of the United States, directly and through our ambassador in Washington. As I mentioned, this was supplemented by the important call that the Prime Minister made to the President. We have exchanged information with the president of Mexico and with the prime ministers of Nigeria and India.
[Mr. Martin (Essex East) .1
I also spoke to the French ambassador in Ottawa and addressed a message, as foreign minister for Canada, to the French foreign minister. The United Arab Republic ambassador called on me on Sunday. This morning I was in close touch again with the Canadian missions concerned. I have also had the advice of Mr. Barrette, the Canadian ambassador to Greece, who is in Ottawa and will shortly be returning to his post in Athens.
The reason for our concern is obvious to the house. The continuation of hostilities in Cyprus could have the gravest consequences for the effectiveness of the United Nations and its peace keeping and mediation roles. The solidarity of NATO as a defence alliance is also being strained. It can be understood, therefore, that the government has felt obliged, particularly in view of the large contingent of Canadian soldiers now serving on the island, to make certain that we were at all times fully informed about the situation and that our views, as the crisis developed, were made known quickly and effectively.
We have had three major objectives during these negotiations; to help in bringing a halt to the hostilities that have so far taken place; to preserve and if necessary strengthen the authority of the United Nations to assist in resolving the crisis, and to prevent the spread of the conflict, keeping in mind all the while the need for action which would, if possible, lead toward a longer term solution of the pressures which produced the crises.
Yesterday afternoon the security council accepted a resolution, put forward by the United States and supported by the United Kingdom, asking for a cease fire. The spokesman for the government of Turkey accepted this resolution, as did the representative of Greece and, with some reservation, the government of Archbishop Makarios. There is a cease fire on the island as of the last moment when I had a chance for a full report. A formal acceptance by the Greek Cypriot government of the cease fire has been received by the secretary general; and while the formal acceptance of the cease fire has not yet been received from the government of Turkey I was advised, just before coming into the house, by the United Nations that this was expected momentarily.
Mr. Speaker, no effort was spared by the government of Canada during these past few days to support strongly action that was being taken in many capitals of the world to avoid the possibility of a war or an extension of the conflict that had already begun on the island of Cyprus. I need not empha-

size our concern in the matter, a concern I know is shared by every member of the house and by everyone in Canada. It is a concern that arises not only because we want to see peace on the island, and not only because we believe the United Nations has an important role to play, but because we realize that an expansion of the war in that particular theatre would have the gravest consequences for the peace of the world.
It is with this thought in mind that I make this preliminary report on the efforts of the government during the past few days with regard to this critical situation.

speakeroldname: Righi Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I begin by associating myself with the sentiments of the Secretary of State for External Affairs concerning the need of everything being done that our country can do, that the United Nations can do, that members of NATO and of the commonwealth can do to bring about a cease fire on the island of Cyprus, and ultimately by mediation to bring about a settlement of the differences that have caused so much internecine strife in the past few months.
The minister has set out in some detail what the government of Canada has endeavoured to do in recent days to bring about a solution of this problem. When events like this grave and dangerous to the peace of the world take place governments have resting on them grave responsibilities. Recently I read a book "The Last Ten Days", dealing with the ten days prior to August 4, 1914, from which one can only conclude that if the nations then in disagreement had pressed forward their efforts toward peace, instead of more or less surrendering to what many regarded as inevitable, the first great world war might have been avoided. We meet today in circumstances serious to the preservation of peace, serious because of their danger to the potential spread of war.
Unless a solution of the problem in Cyprus is attained we face a weakening of the United Nations as a world organization. We face as well the undermining or at least the weakening of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, an organization that rests its eastern flank upon the assurance that Turkey and Greece shall, as members of that organization, carry out their responsibilities. Indeed, without them NATO could scarcely survive.
We hope there will be a cease fire that will be effective. The minister has advised that since passage of the resolution of the United Nations security council on Saturday
Cyprus Crisis
there has been no resumption of attacks by Turkish forces, and that there is relative quiet on the island.
The basic problems as I see them today are these; to bring a check to the increasing hostility between the Turks and the Greeks and, also of great importance, to prevent the communists from exploiting this critical situation in Cyprus to their own ends. I do not intend to say anything which would indicate any division of opinion in this house among its members, or anything which would weaken the unity of our country at this time. We are placed in a position where the situation in Cyprus challenges, as I said a moment ago, the unity of NATO and the continuance in strength of the United Nations.
However, I do wish to refer to one matter which has been raised on more than one occasion in this house by Her Majesty's loyal opposition, and that is the question of the empowering of our troops as members of the United Nations force to discharge the responsibilities which were placed upon them. The question has been asked in all parts of the western world, how has it come about that the United Nations has not been able to bring an end to the continued hostilities on this island? Is it because for reasons which have not yet been explained the power of the United Nations force was not that requisite to discharge those responsibilities?
Over the week end various influential world newspapers have dealt with these questions and I think, generally speaking, the viewpoint has been that of the New York Times as expressed in yesterday's edition:
Three months to the day after the British began patrolling Cyprus, the United Nations force, with a strong British contingent, went into operation.
It has been tied down to restrictions, without the authority of search and disarm, and able to move about only with the permission of the Greek Cypriots. Often under fire from both sides, some of the Scandinavian contingents have threatened to leave unless they are given some authority.
Over and over again this point is driven home, the need for the force under the United Nations to have an authority which it has not possessed heretofore.
I have before me pages from Hansard which record from week to week the raising of this point by the official opposition. Too often, I am sorry to say, it was brushed aside. You will recall, sir, that I stated on one occasion that 4,000 Greek troops had landed surreptitiously upon the island of Cyprus; that the United Nations force was almost emasculated by lack of power to prevent landings, lack of power to disarm and, above all, by

Cyprus Crisis
lack of power to move freely. I could quote numerous occasions upon which this has been referred to, but I will restrict myself to one or two. On June 9 I asked whether there was any imminent danger of an outbreak of war. I also asked:
Has the Canadian government, as a government which has made a great contribution to Cyprus in the peace keeping force, made clear to President Makarios its strong feelings at his reported statement-and I am going to keep within the limits of parliamentary speech-that he would be calling upon the U.S.S.R., or would welcome the U.S.S.R., to settle a matter which is particularly dangerous at this time?
The answer given by the minister of defence was uncertain. In general it was the answer given again by the minister on the same day when he stated "The department has tried to take all possible contingencies into consideration".
On June 26 I again raised this question and again the government's answer was uncertain. I do not want to say it was evasive, but if I were to use that expression it would describe the degree to which parliament was denied information. It was on July 2 that I referred to the Greek troops landing. The minister's answer on that occasion was:
I cannot say whether the press reports mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition are exactly in accordance with the facts. There are reasons for believing, however, that there have been importations of one kind or another. Beyond that I do not wish to go at this time.
On July 3, when this question was again raised, the minister had this to say:
The hon. gentlemen-
-he was referring to me-
-yesterday gave a figure of some 4,000. X could find no justification whatever for that figure. The information I already have obviously implies that there have been importations of arms and of bodies, and we have taken strong exception to this.
Again there was uncertainty. However, if importations were taking place clandestinely, as was subsequently established, surely that was the time to have heeded the views of the opposition, in the interests of Canadian troops serving in the United Nations force, that they should be empowered to prevent such things taking place.
On July 7, in reply to a further question, the minister expressed the same view:
We have studied the allegation and the figure mentioned. This question has been investigated by the United Nations itself. The United Nations authorities do not agree with the figure.
All these answers would indicate that the figures I placed before the house-and I do not place these matters before this house
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
loosely in my position of responsibility-had exaggerated the danger created and the number of people landed in Cyprus from Greece. Subsequent events have certainly upheld these fears about the perilous situation created by the troops which did, in fact, infiltrate.
So, on it went. Week after week questions which we asked in this regard were brushed aside. On July 13 I again referred to some 4,000 Greek troops clandestinely landed in Cyprus, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs said:
With regard to the first part of the question there are, as I said last week, different assessments of the infiltrations, and these are now being examined by the United Nations. Until such time as the final assessment has been made I think it is not desirable that I should go beyond what I have already indicated in the house.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I pointed out that this was a matter serious and dangerous to the preservation of peace there and, more particularly as a Canadian, detrimental to the discharge by the Canadian United Nations [DOT] forces of their responsibility. We had more than an academic interest. I am not sure of the figures, but on the basis of the best computation I can make this country has expended $75 million to $90 million on peace keeping operations and the like since the United Nations was set up. This is far and beyond the contribution that could be expected under normal circumstances from a country of Canada's population; far and beyond what would have been anticipated as our share of the forces in Cyprus. Eleven hundred men were provided. When forces in those numbers are provided there is a responsibility on the part of the government, representing all the people of Canada, to assure that those forces shall not have their efforts rendered nugatory by the people in Cyprus.
So throughout the picture the answer was generally the same, "All is well. There is no reason to become aroused. Peace, to all intents and purposes, has been established in Cyprus". Again, with regard to requests that were made for the enlargement of the powers of the force, the same answers were given. Finally on July 23 I said, among other things:
Some weeks ago it was suggested by members of the opposition that rules should be promulgated which would empower the United Nations force in Cyprus to prevent what has actually occurred since, namely incursions by troops from outside the country.
Then I went on to ask whether new rules would be established. Again the answer was,

in effect, "All is well. Be not disturbed; the government is giving the fullest attention to these matters. Phone calls are being made, statesmen in other countries are being interviewed". Those actions, estimable as they are, do not provide the power to a United Nations force to discharge its responsibilities. Now we find that, in part due to the failure to insist on extending the powers of the United Nations forces, several thousand men have infiltrated the island. There was the attack the other day by the Turkish air force from without; justified by Turkey on the ground that it was an operation to preserve the Turkish minority. This would not have taken place, as I see it, if the United Nations force had had the authority to act. But here we have forces supplied by Canada, the expenses paid by Canada-an extraordinarily good force, the Royal 22nd, with a proud tradition-as helpless as if they were non-existent because they lack the power to act. That is not overstating it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: It is overstating it.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The Scandinavian countries made it perfectly clear that they were not going to have their forces pushed around and placed in peril. They threatened that they were going to leave unless powers were given to their forces to carry out the mandate they had received.
I would like to have further information. The minister is going to speak again, and I would like him to take the house into his confidence. There is no question of security here. I do not want to see security in any way invaded, but there is no question of security in answering this question. Why were these extra powers not granted? They were asked for by the various forces. Why were they not granted? For too long we have simply been lulled into a false sense of security regarding this matter by explanations, by words of self praise by the government. The time has come now to give this house the facts. I repeat what I said earlier. We joined with the government in complete unity to bring about the dispatch of this force. We want the government to assure that the force Canada sent and has there shall have the necessary power to do that for which it was sent and for which we as Canadians pay.
The Minister of National Defence went to Cyprus. He went; he saw; he returned. But the house received nothing but a general summary of the situation, no more than the country received last night when the minister
Cyprus Crisis
appeared on television. We want information; not information that in any way will undermine security, but information that will remove the smokescreen of silence with which we have been faced throughout the past three months.
The Minister of National Defence smiles. I would ask any hon. member in this house to read the records of Hansard. His smiles do not appear there; if they did, there would at least be some information that has not been vouchsafed to the house up to the present time. His statement last night, if I took it down correctly, has become almost a shibboleth; the words were "All eventualities have been taken into account". That is what we have heard for the past three months. That is the type of answer that we in this house have received after questioning, but we have not had that information to which we are entitled and which I hope on this occasion we will get.
What a terrible situation it is, involving our two allies, Greece and Turkey. I think the house as a whole will commend Prime Minister Papandreou of Greece for his outspoken statement the other day when he reminded Archbishop Makarios of the need of preserving and maintaining the peace. They are our two allies. Can we dare permit them to fight one another with weapons supplied to strengthen defence against communist aggression? That is how serious is the problem.
What can we do now, Mr. Speaker? It is not for me on this occasion to suggest alternatives; that is too late. But in addition to the fact that the United Nations forces have not the necessary authority, I believe it can be said that their numbers are also too small. I suggest that some of the other nations in the United Nations, even now, make available further troops. If up to three weeks ago the number which infiltrated was 4,000 in addition to the forces already in the island, 7,000 United Nations troops are insufficient to carry out their responsibilities to end the ground fighting and to keep both sides from strengthening themselves with arms and trained men imported into the country.
What has been done in that connection? We should like to have the necessary information. As I said at the beginning, the danger to the peace of the world which would be occasioned by two of our leading allies going to war would be frightful in its import with regard to the hope of containing communism.
What of the United Nations? Is it becoming weaker? Within the last few days the U.S.S.R. has indicated, through Mr. Khrushchev, that if

Cyprus Crisis
the U.S.S.R. is required to pay its assessments it will withdraw from the United Nations. That I do not believe. I think that is the usual bluff, similar to that which he endeavoured to practise over the Berlin wall. But if perchance it is not, where will the United Nations be if it adopts or permits two standards, one for the powerful and the other for the rest of the United Nations? I think what is happening today is a great challenge and threat to the peace keeping capacity of the United Nations. The United Nations force in Cyprus dare not fail. I have seen references to the possibility that the Canadian contingent might be withdrawn. Such a withdrawal would be one of the major defeats of the United Nations-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
-and it would take years for that organization to recover. In saying that I again emphasize the fact that just setting up United Nations forces and giving them a name and a blue beret will not keep the peace. There must be an authority given by the UN to enable that force properly to carry out its responsibilities.
The next thing, as I see it-and, as I would have expected, the government has acted in this regard-is to expedite the mediation of the immediate differences in order to bring about a cease fire which will be one in fact as in name. The next difficulty will be-this is the larger one-to reach a long time solution acceptable to Greece and to Turkey and to the people of Cyprus. In this regard, sir, many alternatives have been offered. The meetings in Geneva have as yet, as far as the members of this house know, achieved little or nothing. Makarios is not represented there, as I understand it. Unless he is represented any tentative arrangements have no effect.
All of this is looking into the future. Our immediate responsibility is to do our part to assure an end to strife on the island. It is hard for a Canadian to understand how on such a small island it is possible to develop such bitterness as exists between the Turkish and Greek Cypriots. Certainly the constitution that was accepted by them, in light of the events since its adoption, has proven itself inoperative. We have heard, Mr. Speaker, a lot about constitutions in our country, but I am sure none of us would like to see a constitution adopted under which a minority of 20 per cent can determine by its veto what shall be the laws of the country. The minority must be protected and assured

of its rights so long as the constitution is in effect. The minority must not be subject to being stricken down by the majority. The minority must not be permitted to be thirsted into submission, as is alleged by the residents of one of the major towns in the northwestern part of Cyprus. They can be protected only by a United Nations force that is a force in fact as well as in name.
We as Canadians sent our forces to preserve the peace, and to emasculate them by denying them the power to do so has been proven unjustified by events. Even now I impress on the government the need for doing everything it can do, which it has denied has been necessary for three long months; namely, to place this United Nations force in a position where it can do that which it is required to do, and do it effectively. We can trust our forces not to act in a belligerent manner even though they have these extra powers. We cannot trust them to be able to do their job unless they have the tools. Give them the tools and they will do it.
That has been the request from the opposition for all these months. Now in the light of events we can only say that whatever the obstacles may have been to giving them that power, they should be removed and it should be made clear to the United Nations that Canada, willing and desiring to help in the course of international peace, does not approve of placing her forces in a position of vulnerability without the power to act when it is necessary to do so.
I cannot conceive of any hope for peace in Cyprus, in sending out troops as a police force, yet wearing blinkers so they cannot see what is going on. They are denied the opportunity of moving in the places where their authority is being undermined. The situation is as simple as that.
Mr. Speaker, I conclude by expressing the hope that this house will continue to give its support to peace keeping operations in the interests of world peace. Canadians are beginning to ask this question. Why should we as Canadians take unto ourselves not only the provision of the forces but the payment of the forces, yet when it comes to giving them the normal authority they should have, it is not given. We want this force to carry out its responsibilities. We do not want our forces subjected to the humiliation of being pushed around because they lack the authority to do those things that are necessary. Above all we want them to have that freedom of movement which we are informed they have but in fact they have not.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his opening remarks the Leader of the Opposition said that in times like these governments carry grave responsibilities. Of this we are all aware. I think it might also be said that during a week end such as we have just had the government in what it has tried to do has acted not just on its own behalf, not just on behalf of the party that happens to be in power, but on behalf of Canada as a whole. Likewise, I am sure the Leader of the Opposition in precipitating this debate this afternoon did so in order that parliament as a whole might speak with respect to this very important question.
It is my hope that when this debate is over, however long it may last, its main note will turn out to be that Canada strongly supports what the United Nations is doing in trying to achieve peace in Cyprus and in so doing to save the peace of the world. It is inevitable that in a debate such as this questions will be asked, some of them critical. I hope those questions will be answered. It is inevitable that criticisms will be expressed but, as I have already said, I hope that the crowning note of this debate will be one of Canada's support for the United Nations.
Mr. Speaker, throughout yesterday the people of this country, in common with people throughout the world, were concerned lest we be engulfed in the flames of a third world war. We were very alarmed when one of the bulletins during the day used that very phrase as coming from the mouth of Archbishop Maka-rios. We are, of course, relieved that the tension seems to have subsided a bit, and I think it is well for us to remind ourselves of the outstanding fact of the situation which surely is this. The reason the tension has subsided, the reason this crisis has not already broken into a world war, is that the United Nations has been able to deal with the situation. It has been able to do so two ways. On the one hand it has had its peace keeping force, whatever its limitations may have been, on the island of Cyprus since last March. Even though that force may have been too small to cope with the much larger numbers of armed persons on the island, whether regulars or guerrillas, and even though it may not have had the kind of authority the Leader of the Opposition feels it should have had, I suggest that its presence there during the months since March of this year has played a part in preventing the outbreak of the kind of hostilities that could have flared into a world war.
The other way in which the United Nations has been able to deal with this situation, as has already been referred to by the Secretary
Cyprus Crisis
of State for External Affairs, has arisen from the fact that the security council has been in
session.
Mr. Speaker, we are often disappointed at the slowness of progress in achieving the peace of the world. We are often disappointed in the United Nations, but I think it has to be said that every time a threat of war does arise that it is a tremendous thrill to be able to turn on the radio or the television and see representatives of the potential antagonists sitting around a table, perhaps calling each other names but, nevertheless, discussing the matter before war breaks out. I think we can take pride as members of the human race in that we have made at least this much progress and do have the United Nations in existence to deal with situations of this kind.
It does seem to me that as Canadians we should be very proud of the fact that we are participating in both of these aspects of the United Nations activities in the present crisis. We have our men in the peace keeping force in Cyprus and although we are not at the moment a member of the security council of the United Nations we have our permanent representative there and, as has been reported to us today, our government officials have been keeping in close touch with the situation.
I think that in any assessment of this situation we should be conscious of how difficult the operation in Cyprus is. We knew that before we agreed on March 13 to send our troops as part of the United Nations peace keeping force. I appreciate the feelings of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) when he speaks of the fact, as he spelled it out in his motion, that he feels the forces there do not have sufficient authority to act effectively. But I suggest we should also remind ourselves of the fact that it was necessary to get the consent of the government of Cyprus in order to place the United Nations peace keeping forces on that island. If the United Nations had to engage in a certain amount of bargaining as to what the terms of reference would be to get the forces on the island, let us be grateful we have got them there. If the United Nations had held out for terms of reference to which the government of Cyprus would not agree and as a result had had to choose between shooting its way on to the island or not going there at all, I suggest that by now the crises we have had might well have flared into full scale war.
I urge that we appreciate the difficulties involved in this whole operation. Peace keep-

Cyprus Crisis
ing is something different from war itself. The troops that one sends into a peace keeping operation must of necessity have different terms of reference, and this whole situation is quite different, for example, from the United Nations effort in Korea a few years ago. While I agree that every effort should he made to get the United Nations to win, if possible, the most effective terms of reference for the peace keeping force in Cyprus, I do feel that we should not be indulging today in a castigation of the United Nations for having failed to get the kind of terms of reference that some people feel they should have. That is the reason I sounded the note I did at the beginning of my remarks. My feeling is that the world is grateful that the United Nations has been able to do as much as it has, and I think that the word today from Canada's parliament should be one of support for the world organization.
The Leader of the Opposition said something else today with which, like his words which I quoted earlier, I am in complete agreement. He said with respect to the United Nations peace keeping force in Cyprus that it dare not fail. He is absolutely right. This peace keeping operation must succeed. What is involved in this peace keeping operation is not only the achievement of a real cease fire on the island of Cyprus and hence the avoidance of world war at this time, but also the success of the whole idea of peace keeping operations on the part of nations of the world on a collective basis.
We Canadians have a right to be proud of the part we have played in just about all the peace keeping operations of the United Nations and I think we have a right to be proud of the part we have played in Cyprus. I agree that other nations should have joined with us. I agree that the amount of the cost we are called upon to pay is disproportionate. But, Mr. Speaker, if others were not prepared to share the burden, if it had to be borne by Canada, this is a chapter in our history of which we can be proud. We tend to boast of the glories of our history in one war after another in the past. I suggest that operations of this kind that are aimed at turning the threat of war into peace, that are aimed at finding ways to maintain the peace of the world, are the kind of operations of which we can be most proud.
So, Mr. Speaker, we welcome the opportunity for this debate which has been provided by the motion made by the Leader of the Opposition. We were happy to agree to the suggestion that the Secretary of State for 
External Affairs (Mr. Martin) might be permitted to make an initial statement and that later he might answer the questions put to him. We trust he will take advantage of that opportunity. But when all is said and done it is our hope that on behalf of the Canadian people Canada's parliament will say today: We rejoice in what the United Nations has been able to do in the past few months, we rejoice in what it was able to do over the week end, and we pledge to that world organization our full and wholehearted support.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is the unanimous opinion of all members of the house that the situation in Cyprus is most critical. Not only is it critical as far as peace on that island and relationships between Turkey and Greece are concerned, it is also critical in relation to peace in the Middle East and in the entire world. Therefore it is good that at this time we should have the opportunity to discuss the situation in Cyprus in more detail than would otherwise be allowed and, indeed, the whole position of the United Nations and peace keeping arrangements throughout the world.
I think it is also the general opinion of most members of the house that the United Nations is far from that ideal organization we would like to see in view of the over-all world picture. I along with others have often been very critical of the United Nations and the part it can play effectively in maintaining peace and permitting the peaceful development throughout the world to go forward as it should. However, as I have watched the situation in Cyprus right up to the present time I believe we must admit that the cease fire arranged yesterday was arranged only because the United Nations was in existence. No one else could have done it and I admit that any cease fire permitting more satisfactory negotiations for a permanent peace can only be brought about through the United Nations. Perhaps even the United Nations will not be able to do it, but certainly no other organization has any chance of doing it. Therefore in this situation I believe it is essential for us to maintain the same vigilant and diligent attitude toward events on Cyprus but at the same time recognize facts as they are, principal among these being that the United Nations deserves and must have our support now.
The leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) has been very critical of the fact that the United Nations really does not

have any teeth and thus does not have any authority to take effective action to keep events from happening such as have happened in the last few days. But we must realize that the United Nations cannot force itself upon anybody. A peace keeping operation of the United Nations, such as we are presently participating in, can only take place with the assent of those responsible for government in the areas concerned.
We all admit that our troops are handicapped in doing the job they would like to do and as it should be done, but the reason they do not have the authority is not due to the United Nations. It is because the government of Cyprus has refused to give them this authority or let them assume it. Unless you move a United Nations force in by sheer force of arms which, after all, is not the function of a peace keeping force, there is no alternative but for it to operate on the basis which the force on Cyprus is operating.
The leader of the official opposition has also been rather critical of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), and I do not intend to plead the latter's case in any way at all. In fact, for a number of months after he assumed office I found myself wondering why he never got up and really got going on some of the things he used to talk about, and which Canada has an opportunity to do. But in relation to this instance concerning Cyprus it seems to me everything that was possible to do has been done. In fact, as I read the press and hear the reports from overseas, it seems that it was due to the leadership Canada gave that as much was done as has been done.
We can turn our minds back to March 13. If it had not been for the insistence of Canada, if the United Nations had not been prodded into action, if forceful action had not been taken by the Secretary of State for External Affairs himself in going to New York and attending the United Nations, the peace keeping force would not have been brought into existence and we would be in the middle of a war right now. While we have regrets about the difficult situation in which our peace keeping soldiers find themselves, let us remember that if it had not been for the initiative Canada took in seeing to it that the peace keeping forces got over there, we might well be in the middle of a world war. In fact the ultimatum Turkey gave on that eventful Thursday morning, March 12, which resulted in the precipitation of definite United Nations action, was a point far closer to war than most of us
Cyprus Crisis
recall or may have been aware of at the time. I am sure if our forces had not gone over, even though their authority was limited, that ultimatum would have been acted upon and would have brought us into a far greater crisis than we are in at present.
Something else which is essential in a situation such as we face today, a situation we could well face at any time in southeast Asia, and which could even blow up in Africa, is that we must maintain as cooperative an attitude as possible in these matters, in order that we can present a united front and not let partisan things come between our own image and the force which we can contribute in playing that special role which is Canada's in situations like this.
Therefore I feel that even though the Secretary of State for External Affairs has not given us all the information we would have liked to have, in many cases it has been because he has been unable to give it, or because it has not been in the best interests of what the United Nations has been trying to do. I have found myself very frustrated during the last three or four weeks when we became aware that the Greek Cypriots were moving military equipment into Cyprus and that a build-up for deliberate military action was taking place. Yet I found myself having to agree with many of the statements that were given in this house, simply because there was no other action that could be taken, short of armed intervention.
I also believe we tend to lose sight of the fact that for the past three weeks at least negotiations have been going on in Geneva, and that behind the scenes all possible action has been taken. It is not only the United Nations mediator who has played a leading part in these negotiations, but also the representatives of the two nations that can have positive influence in the situation, Great Britain and the United States. I am speaking of Lord Hood and Dean Acheson.
We must not minimize the critical situation that confronts us, but at the same time I am sure all of us admit that the United Nations has done as effective a job as it could have on Cyprus, under what are probably the most difficult circumstances it has ever had to face in trying to set up a peace keeping operation. We must also face facts as they relate to the situation in Cyprus itself.
I find some reason for optimism today in this situation in that Russia, in replying to Turkey regarding the alleged attacks by its air force yesterday, has taken upon itself, to

Cyprus Crisis
warn Makarios himself and the Greek Cypriot government of what might happen if they continue on as they have been doing. Likewise it is of some encouragement to note that the Greek government has not given its wholehearted support to the Greek Cypriot government on the island, as it might well have done.
Today we have learned that for the past week or so no arms or military equipment have arrived on Cyprus from Greece. One of the things Greece must answer for is the fact that it had a very major hand in permitting 3,000 or 4,000 people to land on Cyprus several weeks ago, a point which was referred to by the Leader of the Opposition. But in this immediate instance at least, Greece is realizing there is a limit beyond which she cannot go unless she becomes swamped in a world war from which she could not benefit, due to the superior military might of Turkey and the attitude other NATO countries would be bound to take if such a conflagration should actually arise.
This brings us back once more to Cyprus, and I think the focal point of the current problem there is this man Makarios, Archbishop Makarios, who is to blame for what has been taking place in Cyprus, and the fact that the United Nations forces there do not have any more authority than what they have presently is something that must be laid right at his feet.
One of the disturbing elements that centre around the leader of the Greek Cypriot government is the type of men with whom he has surrounded himself. One of these is the young man, Nicos Sampson, a former guerilla gunner, who has great influence on policy so far as the government is concerned. Another is General George Grivas, who commanded the Greek Cypriot guerillas in the fighting that took place in the days prior to independence. Just what part Grivas is playing and what connections he had, or still maintains, with the Greek government, and what he is doing in Cyprus, are questions which I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs will propose to the United Nations as being important to determine.
Another man who I think is very dangerous-and this brings us to another aspect of the Cyprus situation-is Dr. Vasos Lys-sarides, a medical doctor who is probably the most radical of all the political extremists on the island, a professed communist and a member of the communist group in the Cyprus house of representatives. Unless people such

as these have pressure brought to bear upon them so that they realize the danger they are creating by their extremist attitude there cannot be any hope of a permanent solution in Cyprus short of intervention by force. I am sure that in the negotiations which have been going on in the past few weeks all these things have been taken into consideration. On the other hand, we are now reaching a point where the cease fire which was arranged yesterday could blow up at any moment and we might find ourselves in extreme difficulties in consequence.
I take a certain amount of confidence in statements such as the one made by the former commander of the United Nations force, General Gyani, when he said the United Nations had done the maximum possible. He said this some weeks ago when he turned over the command of the United Nations force to his successor. 1 think it is essential we should realize, also, that in this Cyprus situation there are other forces at play, besides those inherent in the difficult situation on the island itself. I am not sure whether or not this has been verified, but certainly much of the military equipment which has poured into Cyprus in the last few days has not originated in Greece but has originated in other countries in the Middle East which, for their own advantage, are playing this situation up with all the political opportunism of which they are capable.
We have no alternative but to admit that we have given the United Nations peace keeping machinery one of the most difficult assignments it has ever undertaken. We are facing a situation which is more explosive and more threatening to world peace than even the situation in southeast Asia. At this time the only hope we have of maintaining a cease fire and reaching some kind of settlement is through the United Nations. I would assure the secretary of state, therefore, as he continues to play an aggressive role in this affair, that he has our support. I do so because I think he is aware of what is involved in these problems, and also because I believe there is no alternative. So, though we wish to be kept informed to the fullest possible extent, we are bound to agree that those who have the responsibility in this situation must be trusted to use their best intelligence and act in all cases with integrity.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, the newspapers as well as radio and t.v. brought us news about the crisis in Cyprus. We were told that American-built

Turkish jet aircraft which formed part of the NATO forces' establishment were attacking Cyprus. In addition, we were informed that Greek jet aircraft, also American-built, were getting ready to defend the Greek Cypriots against United States-made jets belonging to Turkey. At the same time, the possibility was mentioned that an American squadron might take up position between the two groups with American-built United States aircraft, still against troops or planes which are part of NATO.
I believe it would be a good thing to start asking ourselves questions about the weapons used to wage war or spread trouble in that area: Greece, Turkey and Cyprus.
It is all very well and perhaps admirable for an American delegate to the UN to call for a cease fire but, in my opinion, the United States should first stop providing weapons to those who open fire; that might be the best way to obtain a cease fire.
There are questions which should be asked concerning the trouble in that part of the world. Mention is being made of the powers of the forces, including the Canadian forces, which are operating in Cyprus under the United Nations. But now, in Cyprus, we see armed fighters, and guerillas. The United Nations troops cannot even disarm them. New weapons are even permitted to come into Cyprus. In that case, what is the United Nations peace force doing in Cyprus if it cannot even disarm the fighters.
No government in the world would accept that within the limits of its territory, there be armed troops and guerillas without trying to disarm them. And yet Archbishop Makarios' Cypriot government is refused the right to do so. At this time, on Cyprus there are, guerillas and rebel troops. The government is attempting to disarm them. Archbishop Makarios' elected government is a democratic government like any government in the world or rather, like many other governments in the world. The government, representing the interests and the majority of the people, is not to have even the privilege of disarming guerillas and rebel troops on its own territory.
When the Cyprus elected government attempts to disarm rebels and guerrillas on its own territory, another country, Turkey, sends airplanes to drop bombs over Cyprus. That is beyond me.
When there were United Nations troops in the Congo, there was also the government of Katanga headed by Mr. Tshombe, a government elected by the people and also a democratic government, but which did not 20220-417
Cyprus Crisis
comply with the decisions of the central authority. That did not prevent the United Nations troops from taking up arms to help the central government to bring to reason another regional government, that of Mr. Tshombe. Then the United Nations forces acted.
Today, in Cyprus, it is not a question of a government which has armed forces, but a question of rebel bands, armed individuals united to fight the duly elected authority. And the United Nations forces are not doing any-think to help the existing government to restore peace on that island.
It is enough to make one wonder what is going on. When the same thing happens in Canada-when a band of rebels start throwing bombs and blowing up mail boxes and buildings, the government immediately calls all the armed forces, the R.C.M.P., the provincial police, the city police. No time is lost in rendering those rebels harmless by putting them behind bars. But when the same thing happens in Cyprus, nothing is done. You are not entitled to disarm the rebels and, not only that, the chief of the Cyprus government is blamed for trying to do it. The United Nations troops are not allowed to do it.
You will surely agree with me that such a situation is not altogether normal. The Cyprus government is not to be allowed to take the means required to prevent the rebels from killing and looting. The Cypriot government is not to take steps to establish peace. United Nations troops are sent to Cyprus without the authority to restore peace in that country. On the contrary, the leader of the government is even blamed when he takes measures in order to restore peace in his country. There is surely something abnormal in that part of the world.
However, the situation exists, and it is essential to understand it fully. If the people are not satisfied with the present government, they only have to vote against it. No election is expected in the near future, but in the meantime, it is the existing authority in Cyprus. If the United Nations want to send a peace keeping force to Cyprus, it must be to help the government of Cyprus so long as it behaves properly. If the authority misbehaves, it is up to the Cypriots to see to it; but in this case, most Cypriots support the government in office.
However, that problem is found in other countries. That problem exists not only in Cyprus but in the United States, our southern neighbour. In Cyprus, there is a problem between Greek and Turkish Cypriots; in the

Cyprus Crisis
United States, it is between whites and blacks. We witnessed similar happenings right at our borders when armed bands went through cities during the night, sacking and looting. The police restored order. The same problem exists in Belgium between Walloons and Flemish, just as that quarrel between whites and blacks in the United States. Ireland went through the same thing and today there is Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland. A solution was found.
History repeats itself continuously. The problem exists since we have been trying to pile up various ethnic groups in one country. It has never worked out. A solution must be found.
Several solutions may come up. First of all, it is inhuman and pagan to say: Let them fight against one another and when there are no more on one side, there will be peace for the other. It is a solution but certainly not the right one.
Another solution would be to try and convince the Greek and Turkish Cypriots to come to terms and reach a sort of friendly understanding. Is it possible to persuade them? Those who are familiar with the situation may have made efforts along that line but, up until now, they have not been successful.
A third solution would be to partition the island, each group being restricted to a designated territory. That might solve the problem and then again it might not.
At any rate, it is not by letting things go on like this or by using a peace force which cannot move and which is powerless that the problem will be solved. On the contrary, appropriate steps must be taken to settle that conflict. It is not by providing weapons or by allowing the infiltration of men and weapons that the problem will be settled.
Mr. Speaker, we must get to the core of the situation. There are solutions to the problem. An identical problem has been settled between the state of Israel and the United Arab Republic. A peace force was sent over there and, today, there are fewer incidents; United Nations efforts have been successful. So, why not do likewise in Cyprus?
Today, war is taking place because of failure to take the means necessary to prevent it. The situation is getting worse all the time. Therefore, proper steps should be taken and Canada should no longer be asked if it could supply weapons, equipment and money. For what purpose? To twiddle our thumbs in Cyprus? To be prohibited from doing anything?
[Mr. GrSgoireJ
The government should take the necessary steps to settle the problem or our troops should be withdrawn from the island. Let us take appropriate measures to settle the problem and cease to act as mere spectators witnessing a fight between airplanes which, on both sides, are made in the United States.
Let us take required means or let us withdraw. At least, they would cease laughing at us, as it is the case in Cyprus at the present time.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say to the right hon. gentleman that I think his initiative today has been a useful one. I want him to know that I believe we are all agreed in the common purpose that attends the operation of the United Nations peace keeping force in Cyprus. I welcome the criticisms that have been made, which I believe are largely the product of understandable frustration in this very difficult situation. I may be pardoned, perhaps, as the minister who has had the closest association with this problem for some months now, along with my colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), if I say that I myself have not been free from some of the frustrations, and certainly some of the anxieties, which we all share.
I have stated a number of times in this house that it would not be helpful, in my judgment, for me as the Secretary of State for External Affairs to assess blame in the developing situation in Cyprus. Canada has no special interests in the eastern Mediterranean. Cyprus is a fellow member of the commonwealth, now wracked by a bitter communal dispute. Greece and Turkey are our NATO allies and both enjoy strategic positions on NATO's southeast flank. A falling out between them is much to be regretted. In so far as Cyprus is concerned I hope there can be a closer understanding between these two countries.
The Canadian contingent, as I see it, in this island can only be helpful in maintaining peace if the people there believe that Canada is there for one purpose only, and that is, as a member of the United Nations force, to assist in preserving order or something approximating order. That is why, among other reasons, it has not been possible for me from time to time in answer to questions in this house-and I do not complain about this-to give the kind of response which may have been sought, anticipated or desired. I have had to bear in mind a number of considerations. One of them certainly was that

nothing I would say should in any way cause any harm to come to any member of the Canadian force in the United Nations body or, for that matter, to the United Nations force as a whole. While it is not always possible for a foreign minister to explain the reasons for the generality of his language or for what may seem to be an evasion, I hope in the time I have held this difficult assignment I have given increasing evidence of my desire to be as objective in the prosecution of this task as I possibly can.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
While I do not propose to take sides on particular aspects of this dispute, that being the general responsibility that is left with the mediator under the security council resolution of March 4, I should think we would generally agree that there must be, in any settlement that ensues, certain basic elements. These would, I am sure, include a more workable constitutional arrangement than that set out in the 1961 constitution of Cyprus; suitable guarantees for the Turkish minority in such fields as language, education, religion and the administration of justice; and an arrangement which might go some way to meet Turkey's concern that the situation in Cyprus should not develop in such way as to present a threat to its security. These are considerations which I am sure those engaged in negotiations in the United Nations and elsewhere will bear in mind. I am sure they will be considered elementary in the very difficult assignment which the distinguished Finnish diplomat is carrying out as the mediator. He has exclusive authority to provide a solution under the terms of the security council resolution.
Canada has participated, Mr. Speaker, in every peace keeping force established by the United Nations, but one. Canada is also taking part in the three international control commissions in Viet Nam, Cambodia and Laos. We have, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said, an enviable reputation in this area, one which reflects not the point of view of any political party in this house but the consensus of the Canadian parliament, and I believe, that of the people of this country.
We may ask ourselves the question: Why did we agree to participate in this difficult operation? Why did the United Nations intervene in Cyprus, an island of 600,000 people made up of two communities, the Turkish Cypriot community comprising roughly 20 20220-417J
Cyprus Crisis
per cent of the population, and the Greek Cypriot community representing the majority? Both have deep attachments, both historically and at present, to two NATO countries, Greece and Turkey. Why should Canada join in trying to provide stability and peace on this little island? This is a question which many people in these days of difficulty have asked themselves. Our response has been given in the speech of the right hon. gentleman and in those made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson). I also well remember that, in the speech which the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) made several months ago when this force was established, we found the raison d'etre for our participation in the United Nations force in Cyprus.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: What is that reason?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The reason was, as the hon. gentleman for Lapointe said, because it was felt that in this interdependent period there was no other way of providing for peace except through the collective effort of the United Nations. While he did not reaffirm that today, his statement on that occasion is one which I think he would still want to maintain.
Now, Mr. Speaker, why did we intervene at that time? It was because there was an appeal from the parties, admittedly on different grounds. There was an appeal from Greece, Turkey and even the government of Cyprus to the United Nations for assistance in restoring peace in Cyprus between the warring communities. There was also a threat of Turkish invasion. The United Kingdom sought urgent United Nations assistance. Its troop resources were overstrained and under severe pressure in trying to keep the peace. It will be remembered that last January there was talk of a commonwealth peace force for Cyprus. There was discussion of a NATO peace force for Cyprus. We in Canada took the position, as we told the British prime minister and his foreign minister when they were here, that while we regarded our responsibilities both to the commonwealth and to NATO as vital, in the event of a peace keeping force for Cyprus we believed that there must in any event be some link with the United Nations, and we made it clear we would prefer a United Nations operation.
What, Mr. Speaker, was the alternative at that time? The alternative was an intensification of the intercommunal strife and probably

Cyprus Crisis
Turkish invasion, followed by Greek intervention and widening hostilities in the eastern Mediterranean. The United Nations in the face of this had an obligation to try to maintain the peace, even though the financial resources of the United Nations, I regret to say, are sadly limited. However a number of countries, believing in international peace machinery- and Canada was among these-agreed to form a United Nations force long before one was established, and others agreed to help to finance it. I well remember on March 12 being in the city of London fulfilling a speaking engagement and receiving a call from the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), suggesting that I should go at once to the United Nations and confer with the secretary general. We had, three weeks previously, given an indication of our willingness to participate in an international peace force, but no progress was being made with the formation of such a body. There would be no international force merely with Canada and one of the coguarantor countries participating. There would have to be at least one other country. No other country had at that point come forward to indicate its willingness to participate in the peace force.
Then while I was engaged in conferring with the secretary general I received a message, which clearly indicated that, but for the action taken by this parliament the next day, and but for the agreements made that night, we might well have had a war in this particular sector. That is why I find it difficult from time to time to understand the criticisms-I am not speaking of this house-which are levelled at the decision of the United Nations to intervene in the way it has through this peace keeping operation on the island of Cyprus.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are many facets in this whole problem. First of all, there is the fact that while this is a peace keeping operation involving the United Nations, it has very important implications for the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, which is our main defensive arrangement in this interdependent nuclear world. We know perfectly well that if there were to be any serious involvement between Turkey and Greece, two countries in the alliance representing this Mediterranean area, it would be a very serious matter for NATO itself, let alone for the peace of the world. It was because of this that the government instructed me to take an active role at the NATO ministerial meeting, impressing upon Greece and Turkey our concern at their involvement, under-

standing, as we did, the reasons why each of them would feel they had some special relationship with one of the two communities on the island.
I would recall to this house, the statement by the secretary of state for the United States, Mr. Rusk, when during that meeting, as later reported and confirmed by him when he said that war between Turkey and Greece in this matter was unthinkable for NATO. No more solemn words I think could have been uttered by the secretary of state for the United States on this particular occasion.
After this meeting we were able to get assurances from these two countries that they would exercise every moderating influence they could on their two communities in Cyprus. The secretary general of NATO, then Mr. Stikker, was assigned the responsibility of a watching brief over the situation. Somewhat later, it will be recalled, the situation began to deteriorate causing the President of the United States to ask the prime minister of Greece, Mr. Papandreou, and Mr. Inonu, head of the government of Turkey, to come to Washington and discuss the matter with him. At that time the government, because of its concern for any involvement by these two countries, accepted my recommendation that I should see both Mr. Papandreou and Mr. Inonu. I again renewed the plea, and then with a special reason, that they should exercise every care and moderation so as not to exacerbate a situation involving not only the peace of Cyprus, and the integrity and unity of NATO, but one which could very well set in motion a chain of events that could have destructive and dangerous global consequences.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I have already indicated the name of the country.
I refer to this incident to show that we felt it was our obligation to inform the secretary general of the situation, and that we had reasons to believe that notwithstanding denials there was a build-up of arms and of soldiers contrary to the spirit and the agreement, or the consensus we had reached elsewhere, in respect to the involvement of these two countries. I may give an example of a difficulty in which I found myself in that regard. At that moment it was suggested in a foreign press that I had indicated there was a build-up, and the suggestion was made in one country or the other that Canada took a prejudiced position with regard to either Greece or Turkey. I think I have been able to satisfy the governments of Greece and Turkey that, notwithstanding what we felt we had to say about this build-up, this could not in any way be interpreted as meaning we favoured one side or another, or that we were proposing any particular solution, because we were not.
Just to show the position facing the government I was greatly concerned for some time that this allegation of partisanship would be
Cyprus Crisis
reflected in the treatment that would be accorded to the Canadian contingent in Cyprus and to the United Nations force in general. I sincerely hope it is now clear that the position we felt we had to take in warning of the build-up has not and will not in any way prejudice the position of our men or the United Nations force itself.
Some will say, what has the United Nations force done? The question could be asked concerning almost any peace keeping operation. What did the United Nations force do in Gaza? What has it done in the Congo? What is it doing in Yemen? What is it doing in Kashmir? I think it is clear that, first of all, if the force had not been established we might have been faced then with an invasion and the possibility of a war, which might well have expanded and engulfed us all.
I do not want to minimize the serious situation which has arisen in Cyprus or the difficulties with which the United Nations force has been faced in carrying out its assignments. I think the record clearly shows, and in this I support the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that the United Nations peace keeping force in Cyprus has made a contribution of great value to the maintenance of stability on the island and to world peace. I remind this house of what Colonel Amy, the Canadian contingent commander, said yesterday that the Swedish contingent was at that very moment saving the lives of hundreds of people in the Man-soura-Kokkina area in the northwest portion of Cyprus, just as Canadians in other days since the force was established have saved human lives on the island.
I may tell the house that if the United Nations were now to give any indication of intention to withdraw there would be the strongest pressure, I am sure, on the part of the three governments involved urging that this would be a regrettable and undesirable course of action.
When the United Nations force in Cyprus was established in March there was, as I say, a very real risk of Turkish invasion and this risk reoccurred a few weeks later. I am not exaggerating when I say that the presence of the United Nations force in Cyprus during the last few months has been one of the factors in reducing a real risk of international war in the eastern Mediterranean that would have shattered the peace, struck a blow to the United Nations and done irreparable harm to NATO.
The United Nations peace keeping effort has likewise during these four months pre-

Cyprus Crisis
vented the resumption of intercommunal hostilities and bloodshed on a wide scale. There was considerable destruction and death over the past few days, but during the period since the force was established, fighting has been only sporadic. As a result the number of fatalities has been lower than was the case before. There have been many incidents, of course, but until the last few days these have been of a relatively minor nature. Even in the most recent outbreak of fighting in the Kokkina-Mansoura area the United Nations peace keeping force has played a valuable role in arranging for cease fires in many localities-I am not speaking now about the general cease fire-and in the evacuation of women and children from the port of Man-soura. Were it not for the presence of the United Nations peace keeping forces in Cyprus, I venture to predict that the hostilities would not have been confined to one area as they have been in effect, but that the whole of Cyprus itself might be aflame today.

Has the minister any information whether or not the government of Turkey

has lodged a very strong protest with the Greek government as at noon today over an alleged raid by the Greek air force on the town of Kokkina?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
There was no raid. The Greek air force did apparently fly over the island and over this particular area. I believe a protest was lodged by the government of Turkey.
There were a number of questions asked, proper questions, and it is my responsibility to answer them. First of all, it was asked in this debate, and it has also been implied in questions from time to time: Why was the force not given greater power than was given to it as a result of the decision of the security council on the 13th of March? First of all, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said, the United Nations has no authority to go and impose itself in any country. We have not reached that stage of international acceptance where the United Nations can automatically assume jurisdiction within the sphere of authority of any particular country. Article II (7) of the charter of the United Nations presupposes that the United Nations is a body of sovereign states. So the United Nations, in this instance as in others, could enter into the peace keeping operation in Cyprus only with the consent of and on terms agreed to by the sovereign power, which is the government of Cyprus headed by Archbishop Makarios.
When the secretary general of the United Nations entered into negotiations with regard to the force he had to meet in part conditions laid down by the government of Cyprus. This accounts in some respects for the limited authority given the United Nations force. But I want to say that generally speaking the authority given the force in Cyprus is comparable to the authority given the forces in the very difficult Congo operation which lasted four years.
