There was no disarming of the population in the Congo, except in one case where there was an insurrection in the province of Katanga. In those desperate days the United Nations did authorize the use of force designed to disarm the special gendarmerie of Katanga province. But throughout the whole operation the United Nations did not seek to disarm, not because this was not in itself a good thing to do but because the United Nations force in the Congo, while larger than that in Cyprus, was not sufficiently large to enable it

to do everything which perfection might have demanded.
When the United Nations forces went into Cyprus there were 40,000 people there with arms. That was the fact. Mr. Hugh Foot, the former governor of Cyprus, has said that he was not able under the British regime to maintain peace on the island with some 30,000 armed personnel.
The secretary general of the UN is responsible for the authority of the UN force on Cyprus and not this parliament. I say that because once this parliament commits its troops to the United Nations, as it has done, the responsibility, subject to consultation, is one that rests with the secretary general of the United Nations. I may say that I have not only argued about this matter with the secretary general but I have discussed it with General Gyani in Geneva, and with the other participating countries. Some have said: Can we not negotiate for further powers, but these could not be obtained in part because it was not possible to get the agreement of the government of Cyprus.
The right hon. gentleman says, and quite properly-I am not criticizing him-that this force is too small. In one sense this is true. If there had been a larger United Nations force on the island on Friday afternoon I am sure that the United Nations might have been able to take strong paramilitary or police action. But the force is under 7,000. The force, under the very terms of agreement with the sovereign power, is limited to 7,000. Even if we wanted to increase it, there is no way by which that force can be increased except with the consent of the authority in charge of the government of the island.
That is a situation that is not unique to Cyprus. It prevailed in every other peace keeping operation. Let us not forget that the relatively successful UN peace keeping operation in the Gaza strip was fraught with all kinds of difficulties when it was established ten years ago. It is now acclaimed by the U.A.R., by Israel and by everyone, but let us not forget the difficulties when it was established. Its numbers were limited, just as are the numbers of the United Nations forces in so many of these peace keeping operations.
We would have liked to see many countries participate in the Cyprus force. Some other countries were prepared to come in. Two other European countries were prepared to come in and participate in this force, but they could not because there were objections by the gov-

I welcome the suggestion of the right hon. gentleman, and I may say it is one that has greatly interested the Prime Minister to see if it is not possible to expand the force if necessary and if the developing situation on the island warrants this. But there again we will be subject to the limitations that arise in a negotiation between one authority that has the power and another that is prepared to render its services, as is the United Nations in this case.
Then someone asks, "Why has the United Nations force not ended the war in Cyprus?" This was one of the questions put forward today, perhaps rhetorically. Well, this is asking a United Nations body to do something no one has been able to do in the course of human history. I hope the time will come when, on the international level, there will be an authority that will enable peace and order to be kept, just as it is being kept today within our respective countries.
There has been a suggestion that from time to time I did not answer some questions, and I think in some instances this is true, but I did this not because I did not want to take this house into my confidence, but because I felt there were proper reasons for taking that particular course. Some information has not been given to parliament, but I say to my hon. friends-not because I am looking for sympathy; I am not; that this is a heavy responsibility which I unreservedly accept. I know I have the good will of the house. There is no parliament of any participating country that has had as much discussion- the record will show this-and has received as much information on this subject as has been the case following interrogations and responses in this house.

I say this is an expense that I am sure we do not regret having accepted. Some day the judgment of our contemporaries and of those who follow will not be disadvantageous to the reputation of present day Canada for having undertaken this particular responsibility.
My right hon. friend says that because we have taken this action, surely we are entitled to some say, and of course we are. I have made this known to the secretary general from time to time, and he has never failed to acknowledge our right to make suggestions to him. I can tell my right hon. friend and members of the house that there have been continuous consultations with the secretary general, with his officers, both those on the 38th floor of the United Nations building, and with his commander and his colleagues in Cyprus itself, in which we put forward our views on particular courses of action.
It is asked, why did we ourselves undertake to pay the full cost of a peace keeping operation in Cyprus? If we had not done that there would not likely have been any peace keeping force in Cyprus. That is the reason.

On March 12 when I discussed this matter with the secretary general, he said "I have no money", and I told him, as the cabinet had instructed me to say, "If there is an international force we will bear our share of the cost." We did this as a means of getting the force into being.
I know that this reflects sadly on the state of the United Nations, but this bankrupt position is not as a result of any position that Canada has taken. We have a different regard for our responsibilities under the charter of the United Nations, which we signed in San Francisco with the Soviet union and every other one of the original members of the United Nations organization.
We agreed to pay the airlift for the Cyprus force ourselves. We agreed to pay the other expenses of the peace keeping operation. Other countries, except Ireland, felt it necessary to receive financial assistance out of the voluntary fund created as a result of the generosity of the United Kingdom, the United States, West Germany and a few other countries. So we have paid our way in this operation because there was no other way out.

Before resuming my seat I want to say that Canada enjoys, not because of any particular political point of view, a reputation for being faithful to its UN obligations. I remember when the Prime Minister and I were visiting 20220-418

General de Gaulle and his foreign minister, the president of that country referred to Canada's idealism and said: "You are idealists". He said that in a complimentary way.
I think it is true that we in the new world do have a point of view which is not always subscribed to by others with a longer history and, in many ways, a greater experience and possibly on that account deeper sophistication in international affairs. But I do believe I reflect not only the temper and mood of this house but the conviction and attitude of most Canadians when I say we recognize in this interdependent nuclear age the futility of war. This forces upon us, now, more than ever, the conviction that justice on the international plane cannot be meted out by an aggrieved nation or its friends. We recall the words of Mr. Justice Holmes when he described how justice had finally established itself in individual communities-how the community "bought off vengeance". That is what we are now engaged in doing-buying off vengeance-so that the international community can assert its authority to dispense justice and to keep the peace.
We must judge Cyprus not by the difficulties of Cyprus, not by the inadequacies of its terms of reference but in the light of a much bigger process of which it is merely a part. There is UNEF. There is the United Nations observation group in Lebanon, our experience in the international control commission in Indochina and the other peace keeping operations in which we have played a part. And now there is Cyprus. These are all parts of a necessary foundation for further peace keeping efforts which will have to be undertaken and in which we shall have to participate-efforts which will cause us anguish but which are essential to the establishment, ultimately, of the rule of law among the nations. That is the reason, that is the justification which must attend our examination of this problem.
We have been lucky thus far in Cyprus. One Finnish soldier has lost his life. We have lost one soldier as a result of an automobile accident. So far, the members of our force have avoided the kind of situations which we have all feared. I hope and trust our contingent will be able to return intact. I would remind this house what we said when we decided to accept the recommendation of the Prime Minister to join in the establishment of this force. I am happy to say that so far this has not been the case. Then he continued:

I hope we recognize that this will be an arduous and a dangerous task and that we ought not to go into it without weighing all its aspects. We did go into this matter with our eyes open. We knew what the risks were. We know what the stakes are. And I say, as one Canadian who has given a lot of his time to the public life of this country: Our soldiers could not be more honourably employed than in working for peace.

Mr. Speaker,
there are a few questions I would like to put to the minister. I will try to make these remarks as brief as I can. There have certainly been rumours in the press since about the middle of June that for a period of about six weeks or so this build-up had been going on. I am sure the government must have had information to this effect, although for quite understandable reasons, when asked about this in the house the minister was rather evasive. I am not blaming him for that; I can understand, having had some experience in these matters, that he had to be, under the circumstances.
I was wondering whether the minister could tell us now for how long the government had been aware and had definite information of a secret nature as to how long this build-up had been going on, and whether they had any details of the kind of troops, materials and supplies that have been going into Cyprus, presumably in this instance from Greece. In addition to that, when this buildup was going on did the secretary general and/or any of the countries such as Canada who were supplying troops to Cyprus put extra pressure on the archbishop to try and dissuade him from carrying on this activity? If any pressure was applied, to what extent was 20220-4184

That is one thing I would like to ask the minister. The next thing is with regard to the present attitude of the president of Cyprus, the archbishop. Now that events have taken the course they have and there is now a cease fire, if I heard the minister correctly a moment ago he said the archbishop was still not complying completely with the terms of the United Nations resolution with regard to freedom of movement. I would hope that now it may be possible to put pretty strong pressure on the archbishop and his government in Cyprus to allow the United Nations the fullest freedom of movement, because if another outburst such as we had over the week end is to be prevented, United Nations troops are going to have to be able to do their job more thoroughly and more completely than in the past. I suppose everyone, including the secretary general, was hopeful that there would not be a blow-up, but when arms build-ups have gone on at the rate they have for the past six or seven weeks it must have been evident that something was going to happen. While I realize that everybody was probably hoping against hope it would not happen, it did.
To prevent a recurrence I think that the greatest possible pressure should be put on the archbishop to allow the UN forces complete freedom of movement so that they can carry out their duties. I would hope that the government of Greece, which has certainly been very moderate in its attitude in the present crisis and as helpful as it can be, could be persuaded to put some pretty strong pressure on the archbishop. Without spending any great length of time on the various viewpoints concerning the attitude and behavior of the archbishop, I think that everyone is in agreement that a great deal of blame, if not all of it, for the present situation can be laid right at his doorstep. If he expects the United Nations to try and keep peace on the island, he should be prepared if he really wants peace to allow the United

Nations forces to carry out their duties according to the terms of the resolution. Now that the trouble is over, we hope permanently, I think, as I have already said, the greatest possible pressure should be put on the archbishop by the secretary general, by Canada and by the other participating countries, and 1 also hope that Greece will do likewise, to try and prevent any more future manoeu-vrings and schemings by that gentleman.
When the debate took place in this house some months ago and this house unanimously decided to send the force to Cyprus, the Leader of the Opposition raised a question concerning the advisability of establishing an advisory committee to assist the secretary general, as was done in the case of the Congo intervention. Apparently that was not done in this case. I recall asking a question about this of the Secretary of State for External Affairs a couple of weeks ago, when he was giving evidence in the committee on external affairs, and his answer was that the secretary general did not wish to have an advisory committee as he did not want to institutionalize that sort of thing. That may have been one reason and perhaps there were others; whether or not the minister can tell us what they were, I do not know. I realize there are some consultative arrangements, as the minister said, but a committee of that type was used to advise on the Congo operation, which everyone now seems to claim was not so difficult. I sat in on a good many of its meetings and I can assure those who say that Cyprus is more difficult than the Congo situation that the Congo was quite difficult enough. We had 15 or 16 representatives sitting around a table discussing this matter at the same time as a great many disputes between themselves were also going on.
One reason I would think that the minister might be able to persuade the secretary general that it might not be such a bad idea to

have a more formal type of advisory committee is that various countries are supplying troops-Canada, Sweden, Ireland. They would, of course, be on the committee, and I do not think it would be too bad an idea if Greece, Turkey and Cyprus were also represented. When people are absent sometimes misunderstandings take place, and it might be possible at such a meeting to put a little greater pressure on some, or one, of the parties concerned. I recall some of the incidents which took place when the Congo operation was going on. The advisory committee met and it was often possible for representatives to put direct pressure on some of the members of the committee, as well as make suggestions. I think some more formal arrangement might be advisable in this case. It certainly would not hurt to try it. You would have all the parties sitting round the table and I think it would be pretty helpful at times.
Another matter is this. The secretary general, who is placed in a very awkward and delicate position from time to time in carrying out and interpreting these resolutions, could get advice from the parties, which might be very helpful. Certainly that was the case in the Congo situation, where the secretary general, the late Dag Hammarskjold, had some pretty sensitive problems to face and decisions to carry out. On such occasions he would ask the advice of the committee, which could be called at a moment's notice, and was on a great many occasions. Very often the suggestions which were offered, while not always accepted by the secretary general, provided him with quite a number of answers and took quite a lot of the burden off his shoulders. I would think it might be very helpful, particularly after the incidents of this last week end, if a somewhat more formal consultative arrangement were made, such as setting up such a committee, which would include on it Greece, Turkey and Cyprus as well as the countries providing troops.
I think these are all the matters I wish to bring up at this time, Mr. Speaker. The minister and others have pretty well covered most points, and I hope that the minister will be able to make some suitable reply.

We have passed through a disturbing, indeed frightening, week end, another one of these crises to which we in our time have become all too prone, if not immune. It followed upon, and was indeed coincident with, another dangerous situation in southeast Asia. We were on the brink of problems the vastness of which perhaps we do not like to explore. There were involved friendly powers, if not to each other at least to us, and the prospect of great power involvements. With the thought of that last dreadful step which we knew was not far away we were all disturbed. Had things become much worse, that grim type of involvement might have been presented to us.
This present issue is very disturbing to Canada because it involves some of the fundamental cornerstones in our foreign policy. I think no one has mentioned the commonwealth-and Cyprus is, after all, a member of the commonwealth. We have discussed the effects of this situation upon NATO, and we have spent a great deal of time discussing that other vital cornerstone of our policy, the United Nations. Canada, as has been said, has been a good and true member, a charter member, a loyal member and an active member of that organization. The record of this body is so much better and more honourable than that of the league of nations that we can have some justifiable pride in the developing pattern of our internationalism. The minister and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Dief-enbaker) were right to point out that our loyalty to the UN transcends partisan politics. We Canadians, at our best, are truly bipartisan in our attitude toward foreign policy. We can all rejoice today that the United Nations is in the picture.
I remember having the opportunity of sitting in the security council chamber-although Canada was not a member of the security council in those terrifying days over Cuba-and I recall how thankful I was that there was still one way out, the next to last arena for settling disputes which can become so explosive they can be no longer handled.
Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak very briefly in respect of a reassessment of the United Nations. I think it is wise, as has been done today, to look at the organization which we so much admire and serve so well. Is the United Nations being weakened? We must never allow the United Nations to become one

of those bodies of fulsome adulation, like the musical banks of Butler which everybody loved and admired, but an institution in which few people placed their faith. We must be analytical and critical. We must make an appraisal which is realistic. I think it is very important, and I say this despite the loquacious eloquence of the minister, that we examine the situation carefully to find out whether or not the peace keeping force is clothed with ample authority. This has been the constant thread of inquiry through all the past weeks and months. I think one can say, without being overly critical, without being an alarmist and without oversimplifying the problem, that much of the difficulty which occurred over the week end stemmed from the fact that the force was inhibited and unable to discharge properly, fully and meaningfully the obligations which should be put upon it. When the United Nations forces was restrained even from observation, let alone prohibitive action, trouble resulted. As the Montreal Gazette in an interesting editorial said, the force went there, not as a fighting force, but when it ceased to be even a supervisory force this great difficulty arose.
We remember how reports came in about thousands of troop landings at a time when the United Nations force apparently and literally was restrained from observing this terrible development. I think the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) was right when he spoke very clearly and candidly, and the Montreal Gazette stated the same thing this morning, that the danger of war would never be removed so long as the matter is left in Archbishop Makarios' hands. With all our desire to be impartial and refrain from even suggesting something which might hurt someone, I support the hon. member in that stand.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) suggested that even now more men may be needed. The minister has told us about all his advocacies all over the world, and I am sure he is a skilled and, if not a succinct advocate, at least a persuasive one. I hope that he will continue to press for more participation by more countries. It is a shocking thing that so few countries were prepared to act in this most important, dangerous and explosive situation. I think also that we must press for clearcut terms of reference. I think if anyone looks back over the records of this house and at the answers given by the minister, he will not describe

Cyprus Crisis
the terms of reference as clearcut, however else one may describe them.
1 have listened very carefully to the very sound and reasonable statements of the minister in respect to the use of force, and I note what he said about the sovereignty of the nation involved. This involved the old concept of international relations, that the rockbed of national sovereignty is something that underlies the whole of international activity. Despite all that, it is a shocking situation when the United Nations force is not even able to observe participation and interference by an outside power. We are now aware that thousands of men were landed in this very disturbing and explosive area and that this occurred without let or hindrance or even observation. There were many days of doubt and denial with rumours rampant but not confirmed. We now know how the balance has been altered and how the situation has become more difficult. Indeed the situation in respect of our own men there, if not precarious, is at least close to it, yet the military representatives of the world body, although not at the vital spot, were there on the island.
Mr. Speaker, we have reached a stage in United Nations development where Canada can speak with authority in respect of the field of peace keeping operations, and at a time when something more is required than that which was given to previous peace keeping groups. Perhaps the time has come to require sufficient strength to restrain warlike overtures of the indigenous armed population, and certainly to prevent the infiltration of those whose intentions are of a warlike nature. How in the world can we expect the Turkish government to be anything but uneasy in view of the reports of additional troops in what the minister has described as "another quarter"? We hope the present breathing space will be sustained-and even at this moment news reports in this regard are confusing-so that not only the immediate mediation, which is so essential, will go forward in fact as in name, but that the long range settlement can be pursued; because that is the other arm of the whole United Nations operation. We do not see the picture clearly or fully if we concentrate only on a military or paramilitary operation.
It is a difficult task that has been assigned to the mediator. Heaven knows that this is a land whose history has many indicators of the kind of trouble which people in Cyprus are undergoing today. History, geography and

facts of world power are things which make the situation in Cyprus extremely difficult and troublesome.
It is a lot easier to desire settlement than to attain it. It is so simple for people to talk about the transmigration of population and moving people here and there, but it is not so easy to enforce these things. We know the constitutional problem. We know the problems facing the NATO alliance and we can perhaps visualize some of the deep emotional feelings that must grip some of these people living daily in the presence of danger, death, hostility, hatred, threats from beyond, and viewed by the outside world as an explosive area which could bring about a holocaust too terrible to contemplate. We are proud of the role of the Canadians there. Canada can be tremendously proud of what it has done in this field. We feel that our men can do their part. But I ask the minister as he has been asked before: Out of his own convictions, recalling that he is the representative of a country which, without immodesty, we can say has done great things in this field, will he not ask for greater authority for this group so that these things will not recur, so that the men wearing the badge of the United Nations will not be shunted off out of sight when dangerous things are going on and when activities with a warlike potential are taking place in the dead of night? He can from a position of great strength continue his argumentation. He has told us he has done so. So he should, and so he should continue with greater vigour. I am confident that the people of the country and certainly the great majority of members of the house will be behind him.
The problem in its acute stage may pass. The headlines may shift to Viet Nam tomorrow and to Berlin the next day, but we all know that the kernel of trouble, is still there. The problem of Cyprus will confront us for a long time. The minister was right in reminding us that we entered into this situation not lightly but with a state of high seriousness in undertaking such a grave step. We must carry on. Whether the people of Cyprus should be removed to their homelands is a matter beyond our discussion today, but they must surely be removed from that deadly daily peril which faces them, and Cyprus itself must be removed as a peril to peace which faces us, which threatens all of us. Through the actions of a stronger United Nations force surely something can

be done so that we will not be faced again with more brinkmanship, more last minute appeals, more hurried telephone calls but will have a force there which will move gradually toward stability at least, if not settlement.
So I would urge the minister to be more outgoing in his reports to the house. He has had an indication today of how the house is behind him in his best efforts. So I say to him: Be more vigorous with your colleagues in the international organization, because you know where the house stands on this matter. We wish him well in his endeavours. We offer these suggestions to him in the hope they will not make his position difficult, nor ours, nor our forces', but that they may strengthen the arm of peace as it is extended through the United Nations.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to discuss the subject that has been raised this afternoon through special motion under standing order 26 in order to bring up what I think are three very important matters in relation to external affairs and Canada's involvement in the United Nations. I think it has been made fairly obvious by the debate this afternoon that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) and the government have almost the unanimous consent of members of the house for the actions that Canada has taken recently and in fact for a long time with respect to peace keeping operations in which we have been called upon to take part throughout the world.
There is one point I should like to raise, and in doing so it is not my intention to try to embarrass the government or the minister or to try to put questions to him that would be difficult to answer. At the same time, however, I believe the people of Canada generally are very apprehensive about what this crisis may do to unity within the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I believe that all members of the house and most Canadians have come to regard NATO as the bulwark standing against the expansion of communism in Europe and for that matter in most of the rest of the world.
When we see two very important members of NATO in a dispute, this has the effect in my opinion of undermining to some extent at least the confidence that Canadians have placed in this great and useful military alliance. I do not wish the Secretary of State for External Affairs to be placed in the position where he has to try to apologize or take
Cyprus Crisis
sides against either one of these two members of NATO, but nevertheless we realize that Greece and Turkey do in fact represent that portion of the NATO alliance covering southern Europe. Therefore if there is to be a great deal of difficulty in that area certainly it will weaken one of the most important positions that NATO has been defending against the expansion of communism.
We realize, as do all Canadians, that the whole purpose of NATO in holding back this expansion is coming into question. As I said, I do not wish to put the minister in an embarrassing position, but at this time there must be a great deal of soul searching going on in NATO respecting the supplying of arms to these two countries. So far as the purpose for which arms and aid have been supplied to both Greece and Turkey, we are assured that both these countries are fulfilling their responsibilities and obligations within NATO, but at the same time I am certain there is apprehension with regard to whether or not some of these arms are now being used for a purpose other than that for which they were supplied.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member but because of the importance of this matter may I point out to him that the supply of equipment by Canada to either of these two countries under the NATO mutual assistance program was suspended when the United Nations Cyprus operation began.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs pointed that fact out to the house several weeks ago. Nevertheless we know that since NATO came into being both these countries have been supplied with a lot of military equipment, and we are a bit apprehensive about what use may be made of it now. For the future I believe that from time to time the Secretary of State for External Affairs and other members of the government should make statements respecting the activities of NATO, so as to assure the Canadian people that this organization's purpose is not eroded as a result of the events of the last few weeks. As I have pointed out, it has always been looked upon as the western alliance for the defence of the free world.
We expect the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the government to follow up as rapidly as possible that which was contained in the letter or note from President Makarios to the secretary general of the United Nations last Thursday night. Until that note was received most of us did not

Cyprus Crisis
know this was the view he would take. Certainly I know of no other time when he indicated his willingness to give free access to United Nations forces.
I have not had time to examine the documents tabled a few minutes ago by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but from press reports it seems there is a disposition on the part of the president of Cyprus to give additional freedom of movement to the UN force, even though this may fall short of complete freedom of movement. Here is another situation where we will have to accept a little rather than all which is asked, and I would urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs and his representatives to state their willingness to accept some improvement in the activities and freedom of movement of the peace keeping force.
Last Friday I asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) if he would give the house a statement respecting the duties, authority, and I even included the limitations on our Canadian forces in Cyprus, so that we and the Canadian people could be assured they would not be placed in indefensible and awkward positions. Here again I realize the delicacy of the situation. I realize it may not be possible to give specific answers, but the ministers should realize there is some apprehension on the part of Canadians regarding the position of our troops, should the situation deteriorate again.
On one or two occasions the Minister of National Defence has informed the house that his department has worked out some program for speedy evacuation of our forces, if necessary. There may be other details, concerning what the government would do in an emergency, that he cannot divulge, but it would be assuring to the people of Canada to know our troops were not going to be caught in an impossible situation.
In conclusion, I have brought up these three matters because 1 think they are important. I do not expect immediate and complete replies but they are matters concerning which I have had some discussion, and have received some correspondence. They are questions the Canadian people are wondering about, and our people at home have a right to as much information as it is possible to give.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think all Canadians were very disturbed over the week end at the events taking place in Cyprus, and very fearful as to what the results might be. Because of this

I think an airing of the matter in the house is desirable at this time.
I am afraid that this afternoon we have had much expression of wishful thinking and of self-deception as to the effectiveness of the United Nations in Cyprus, and of its future effectiveness if the present terms of reference of the force are unchanged. I should like to make it very clear that I am not criticizing the United Nations intervention in Cyprus. Very much the reverse: I think it was a case in which the United Nations had to do everything possible to prevent what has seemed to be, for a considerable length of time, the germ of war developing as a result of the situation on the island.
I was glad Canada sent a force to take part in the peace keeping operation on Cyprus. However I criticize the effectiveness of the operation because the powers granted were not sufficient to enable the force to do the job it should do and must do if peace is to be preserved. I believe this country, the other countries concerned in the operation, as well as the members of NATO and other powers should apply pressure to see that the United Nations peace keeping force's powers are increased.
There is no use in trying to deceive ourselves that the cease fire has come about primarily as a result of the efforts of the United Nations. It has come about because the Turkish aircraft attack and the destruction it caused gave the Greek Cypriots a great deal of reason for pause in the attacks which they had been making on Kokkina and some of the other Turkish villages and enclaves. Had that not taken place I myself am very doubtful what would be the situation now so far as those attacks on Turkish villages and enclaves are concerned. What we want to see is a situation which will ensure that a repetition of that type of attack cannot take place. There is no question but that the risks inherent in the Cyprus operation, the risks to NATO and world peace, are too great to allow any country to stand back and not do everything possible to ensure a conflagration does not ensue.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has stated that the United Nations force was limited in its numbers and limited in its powers because of the necessity to get agreement from the government of Cyprus on both the size of the force and the powers it could exercise. I would submit that at the present time in view of the fact that the Greek Cypriot government has sought unilaterally to tear up the agreement entered into govern-

ing the constitutional situation in Cyprus- an agreement endorsed by Britain, Greece and Turkey-we need hardly be limited to what one might call the niceties of international custom and allow them to stand in the way of sufficient powers being given to the United Nations force in Cyprus to enable it to discharge its peace keeping responsibilities effectively. To do anything else would, in my view, be to do less than we should be doing. It would seem to me that if the NATO countries in particular, who have a particular stake in this situation, along with most of the countries of the United Nations were prepared to say to the Greek Cypriot government that the United Nations force must be increased and given greater powers, this aim could be accomplished.
Turning to another aspect of the situation I should like the Secretary of State for External Affairs to tell us exactly what is the position of the Canadian forces at the present time. Are they still disposed between the Greek and Turkish Cypriot forces, for the most part, or are they assembled in one defensible area in which they would be relatively safe in the event of a full-scale conflagration breaking out? I think, too, we should be told something more definite in connection with the evacuation plans which the minister stated over television last night existed. I think we should be told what these plans are, and told the situation in which it is envisaged they would be put into effect. As I understand it, R.C.A.F. Yukons are on the alert to fly over and pick up personnel fairly quickly. I presume the landing fields over there are safe and would continue to be safe, being in the British enclave. These are matters upon which the Canadian people would like to be assured. Then again, in the event of an evacuation, what is the situation with regard to the equipment which had to be sent over by sea? The giving of these details would not, I think, result for one moment in the impression getting abroad that Canada intended to withdraw her contingent.
As the minister has said, we are committed to this United Nations peace keeping operation, and we are prepared to keep our forces there on that mission. I think the Canadian people should be told, at least in general terms, of the plans which exist for evacuating our forces in the event of a catastrophe which we all hope will not take place, and I think this could be done without any risk or difficulty whatever.

I was
not able to be present in the chamber during
Cyprus Crisis
part of this debate and I hope, therefore, that what I have to say will not prove to be repetitious. I have heard no one make any reference so far in the discussion to the activities of the U.S.S.R. in the context of this Cyprus situation.
If the reports which appeared in the press and over the radio are correct, it would seem that the U.S.S.R. was invited by Archbishop Makarios to intervene in this dispute. Assuming the correctness of further reports to the effect that the Soviet union has given no indication of doing so, it would not be inappropriate I think to make some reference to the restraint with which the Soviet union is, apparently, approaching this situation.
Many of us have been disappointed and- speaking for myself-highly critical of the lack of interest shown by the Soviet union so far in the peace keeping operations of the United Nations, as well as by its failure to assume financial responsibility in this connection. In the circumstances, in the light of the situation historically occupied by Russia, during the pre-Soviet days, the fact that they are unwilling to intervene at the present time, though they may have been tempted to do so, is something which should not go unnoticed in this house. Indeed I think there should be some appreciation of the restraint which has been shown.
We could of course discuss at length the relationship between this lack of interest and the power of destruction which lies in the hands of various nations in the world at the present time. I do not know whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs is prepared to comment on this aspect of the matter, or not. Whatever the reason, it seems to me that the restraint which is being shown is an indication of the direction in which the world is moving, and that there would appear to be at least partial acceptance of responsibility by the U.S.S.R. as a member of the United Nations. I feel sure that in another era, in comparable circumstances, Russian forces might already be moving en masse to intervene in this situation and we in this house, and Canada generally have some reason to be thankful that this is apparently not the case at the present time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The importance of this debate has already been recognized by the hon. members who have spoken and by the interest shown by the House of Commons earlier, resulting in the general agreement that time be given for a discussion of this particular subject.

Cyprus Crisis
We are living in a tempestuous century. Fifty years ago, 30,000 Canadian troops were being collected at Valcartier camp ready for dispatch overseas for the first world war. Since that time we have known scarcely any period in which we have been free from war or threat of war of one sort or another. Last week end we were on a nervous edge again for fear of an outbreak of war in Cyprus which might spread and become a third world conflict. In fact, during the course of this very year, 1964, we have heard nothing, week by week, except reports of threatened war in one part of the world or another. Consequently it is not surprising that the House of Commons should wish to discuss, in particular, the situation in Cyprus and in general Canada's participation in United Nations peace keeping arrangements.
I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) permitted himself to use an expression which he might regret. He was talking about the pride we could show in our peace keeping operations and he said we boast about our history and activities in war. I do not know that anybody boasts about Canada's participation in warfare. I think, rightfully, that as a nation we can take pride in the fact that when freedom has been threatened during this century, Canada has responded and has made the sacrifices essential to maintain that freedom. It is not boastfulness; but surely we are entitled to take pride in the fact that a nation of 8 million people participated right from the very first in the first great war, and a nation of 12 million people participated right from the very first in the second world war, and was not at all reluctant to play its part in Korea. Similarly, in the United Nations peace keeping operations Canada has been in the forefront, with the general approval of parliament and of the Canadian people. Steadily we are setting an example to the world of what needs to be done in order that peace may be maintained. By our actions in the past we have shown that we do not as a nation shrink from the fatal step of war and the sacrifice involved there. Also, during this period we are not shrinking from playing our part in attempts to prevent the outbreak of another world war.
This particular international crisis has, I think, shocked the Canadian people. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) said, it is one small area of the world, an island inhabited by 600,000 people, and to think that one small place like that could be the source of trouble for the entire

world tends to shock people when they think about it. Others have mentioned our dismay that the NATO alliance be endangered by a quarrel arising between two highly respected and important members of that alliance. As a member of that alliance ourselves, we have nothing but regret for the fact that Greece and Turkey are engaged in a dispute over the situation in Cyprus. Also, people are naturally somewhat dismayed to think-and we in the House of Commons share this dismay-that five months of a peace keeping operation in Cyprus has not yet resulted in a settlement, nor in the hope of an early settlement. This is very disturbing, because when we on March 13 agreed unanimously to play an active part in a peace keeping operation in Cyprus under the United Nations, we entertained the hope that within three months a settlement might be arrived at; we entertained the hope that with the appointment of a political mediator the trouble would die down and cease. Yet we are now in the fifth month, our force has been promised for the second three months' period, and this situation may drift on and on.
As was mentioned on March 13 and was repeated today, who could have imagined that eight years after the setting up of the peace keeping operation in the Gaza strip we would be on the job there without a solution in sight. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I wonder why the burden of that particular operation should have been borne all these eight years by Canada. It is not that we object to playing our part in any of these operations, but there is the old fashioned method of taking turns. Why are not other nations engaged in doing a spell of duty in the Gaza strip?
Another reason for our asking for a debate on this issue today is the somewhat less than satisfactory method of attempting to get information over the last five months. I have been looking at the index of Hansard for the end of June; I have not the index of July. There are over 80 lines of entry under the heading "Cyprus" in that index, with quite a number of subheadings following those items; so I would say there have been at least 100 questions asked with regard to our activities in Cyprus. Although answers to questions asked on orders of the day are helpful as we go along, it is impossible to get a complete answer by that method. Earlier we did ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to allot another day for a debate on the subject of external affairs; that was some time ago, and it did not materialize. Today we are having an opportunity to discuss at some

length our peace keeping operation in Cyprus, to express our point of view, to get from the Secretary of State for External Affairs some of the answers and to make evident the attitude of the House of Commons to this particular operation.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the supper hour I was dealing with the inadequacy of the question period on orders of the day to get full information on a subject as important and as complicated as the Cyprus situation. It is not only that the period for questioning is inadequate; some of the answers have not been very satisfactory. I would just give four examples of just how difficult it is to get the information that we require.
On March 13, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) was speaking on this subject, he dealt with the cost in these words, as reported at page 915 of Hansard:
The estimate... of the total costs for three months, including a one-way air lift, is about $2,600,000.
I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs about the cost on July 28, and I was asking only for information because the last purpose I would have in mind was to embarrass the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He seemed to be a bit embarrassed that day in answering my question, but he did reply as reported at page 6063 of Hansard:
I think the total cost of Canada's participation, including the airlift, would be around $24 million for the year.
Then we got, along with others, into a bit of an argument as to whether that was gross or net, and no satisfactory answer really was given. So I would ask, what is the cost of our intervention in the Cyprus affair?
When the supplementary estimates were put in front of us, I asked the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) privately under what items I would find the cost of the Cyprus expedition. He referred me to three items in the supplementary estimates where those costs are included in other costs of the navy, the army and the air force. I think that when a special operation such as this is carried on and requires a supplementary estimate, it would be helpful to the house if
Cyprus Crisis
the supplementary estimate were segregated from the rest so that we know exactly where we stand. I think it is important for us and for the people who generally support our activities in the United Nations, so that other countries who are active, as we are, and those which are inactive will have some knowledge of what Canada's financial contribution is to an exercise such as this.
Another example of an inadequate answer concerned the problem of freedom of movement, about which we have been talking today. On July 28, when the Secretary of State for External Affairs was asked about that matter, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked him this question, as reported at page 6060 of Hansard:
How long ago was it since freedom of movement was first denied United Nations forces, particularly the Canadian force?
This is the answer which the minister gave:
Freedom of access was denied about a week ago.
Then I will skip a phrase and the minister goes on:
-but generally speaking there has been no position taken against freedom of movement, which is one of the essential terms of the agreement based on the understanding between the secretary general of the United Nations and the government of Cyprus.
Later he went on to say:
I would not agree that the United Nations force, by its very presence, is unable to discharge the responsibility which it has assumed. Undoubtedly the denial of freedom of movement impairs its full opportunity to carry out its mandate.
I do not consider that to be a satisfactory answer to questions concerning freedom of movement, because with restricted movement how can the force perform its function at all?
Then on July 31 the Secretary of State for External Affairs was asked about the situation concerning the ports through which aid has been coming in, and his answer, as reported at page 6217, is as follows:
The president of Turkey wrote to the secretary general about a week ago. With regard to the letter of Archbishop Makarios, he also indicates that the United Nations should undertake to supervise not only ports in Cyprus but ports outside that might be considered a source of such shipments.
That is, shipments of arms into the country.
Our view is that there is some merit in this proposal.
I am not sure we have heard from the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether that has been followed up at all. I would have thought from a military point of view that the United Nations peace keeping

Cyprus Crisis
force should have had right from the very-first supervision over the ports of Cyprus. Yet all along we have been hearing about people being landed, arms and munitions being landed, and they can come in only through the ports. The secretary of state I would not say showed indifference to the idea, but all he said was that "our view is that there is some merit in this proposal". Why did he not follow it up with the sternest of admonitions to the authorities at the United Nations and ask permission for our force to take action in the ports?
Then earlier this afternoon when the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) was speaking he questioned the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) about the subject of withdrawal, to which I hope we will get an answer tonight. He was careful to say that having plans for a withdrawal does not mean that panic has ensued or that there is any intention of withdrawing, but that all which is required is a careful plan in case of some emergency.
On March 23 the Minister of National Defence was asked by the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) about this matter, and his reply, as reported at page 1354 of Hansard, was as follows:
May I say again that I hope and expect that it will not-
That is, that there will be no withdrawal. He goes on:
-but 1 am sure our armed forces have demonstrated their ability to be prepared for an emergency and to carry out assignments with noteworthy efficiency and praiseworthy effectiveness.
I challenge anybody to get from that answer anything that relates to the military situation which would prevail in the event of an emergency and our force was withdrawn.
The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) this afternoon asked several direct questions, one of which was to this effect: If withdrawal has to take place do we have a protected airfield from which that withdrawal can be made? How is such a withdrawal to be carried out? Is a withdrawal to be effected by air transport or by ship and what will happen to the military supplies that accompany our force?
I should like to know whether any military appreciation was made of the situation at the time a decision was reached to send Canadians to participate in the United Nations force in Cyprus. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) has indicated that at the time the force was dis-
IMr. Churchill.]
patched 40,000 Cypriot people were in possession of arms. What was the military appreciation under those circumstances? Was it considered feasible that a force of 7,000 soldiers from several nations could maintain peace on that island? I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that the British, who had 30,000 troops there at that time, thought this was too difficult an operation for them. Was the military appreciation, if any was made, to the effect that a peace keeping force of 7,000 men would be adequate under the circumstances?
Since the month of March we have heard repeated stories in respect of the landing of additional arms and equipment on the island. How many thousand Cypriots, either Greek or Turkish, are now in possession of military weapons? Under these circumstances what can be accomplished by a small United Nations force of 7,000 men? The Turkish ambassador said in a statement he made over the radio that 7,000 regular troops from Greece were now on the island. Week by week the position of the United Nations force has become more difficult. I think we are entitled to know exactly what progress is being made, and what is the situation in respect of our own men. In listening to answers to questions asked in this house during the last five months I have gained the impression that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has taken the view that very little must be said, in case the situation becomes worse. However, each week he has made a statement to the effect that things are becoming a little better, yet each week we have received news of further atrocities on the island, culminating this week end in authentic reports of attacks by Turkish airplanes. What progress has been made during the five months that this peace keeping force has been in operation?
On April 30 the Secretary of State for External Affairs tabled a report of the secretary general presented to the United Nations. This report has been reprinted at page 2805 of Hansard. There are ten objectives of a comprehensive program of action for the United Nations force on Cyprus listed in what the secretary general refers to as an annex to his report. He lists also nine interim suggestions for action while some of the other main objectives are being attained. It seems to me the Secretary of State for External Affairs today should have gone through the list of objectives and interim aims as set out on April 30 indicating which ones, if any, have been achieved.

I should like to list a few of these main and interim objectives. The first is:
The task of UN force, as given in the security council resolution of March 4, is to use its best efforts towards the following objectives: (A) to prevent a recurrence of fighting;-
Has that been accomplished?
-	(B) to contribute to the maintenance and restoration of law and order;-
Has law and order been restored?
-	(C) to contribute to a return to normal conditions.
Have normal conditions been restored in that country? There is another list of suggested objectives, the first being:
Achievement of freedom of movement on all roads in Cyprus-
Achievement of freedom of movement for all communities within the whole town of Nicosia-
Progressive evacuation and removal of all fortified positions held by Greek and Turkish Cypriots-
The progressive disarming of all civilians other than the regular police gendarmerie and the Cyprus army by the Cypriot government and the Turkish community.
The arrangement of security measures and other necessary conditions to facilitate return to normal conditions and particularly of economic activity.
I have read just some of these objectives. Have any of them been achieved?
In respect of the interim proposals, have any of the following been achieved?
The removal of emplacements, fortifications and trenches in selected areas of Nicosia-
Has that taken place?
A determined effort in selected areas of Nicosia to re-establish normality by returning to their homes, under UN security guarantee, refugees, as, for example, those from Hamed Mandres to Omor-phita who would not... carry arms-
The institution of the procedures for inquiry into every serious instance of shooting, especially when casualties occur,-
The elaboration of a plan for the reintegration... of the Turkish Cypriot policemen into the Cyprus police force,-
An appraisal of the possibility of establishing in certain areas Cypriot Greek-Turkish-UNFICYP joint patrols as a means of restoring confidence-
I have just read a few of the main and interim suggestions as listed, in respect of which I think we should have been given a report. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has not gone through that list, or given us any real hope for the future.
I should like to refer to two other things in respect of which I would like to have further information. The first has been referred to earlier and deals with the fact that, as the minister has stated earlier, once a force has been committed to the United Nations, authority rests with the United Nations
Cyprus Crisis
and not with the nation providing the force. This is a situation which has disturbed me, and I refer to the lack of effective control by the home government over those forces. I did not think we had sufficient control over our troops on the Gaza strip, and that situation has existed for over eight years. Fortunately no serious incident has occurred there! I was disturbed when we undertook our action in the Congo, but was reassured by the then minister of national defence, General Pearkes, that our signallers who carried only small arms would not be placed further forward than brigade headquarters. Under those circumstances I thought perhaps their safety would be reasonably assured, because signallers cannot carry out their work while at the same time having to post guards and worry about their security.
Nevertheless in the extremely dangerous Congo situation I never felt satisfied in my own mind that we had anything like the control over our forces there that we should have had. In Cyprus the situation is repeated. Our forces are detached from the Canadian army and placed under the command of United Nations officers and we have no control. This is not a criticism of participation in United Nations operations, but I do not think we should be starry eyed about the matter.
Committing men to military operations is a responsibility that parliament undertakes when the government makes a decision, but the safety of these people rests with the government of the country and with parliament. It seems to me that simply to detach them and place them under United Nations control is not sufficient security for our forces. So far we have been lucky in my opinion, but any study of military operations shows that mistakes can be made by high command as well as by junior ranks, and mistakes could be made in one of these operations by the high command.
In many instances we are not familiar with the people who are placed in charge of United Nations forces. We get an account of their military experience. We have confidence that a careful choice has been made. But this does not remove responsibility from the government of Canada or from parliament for the safety and security of our own forces. Using the fairly substantial lessons that we have had over a period of quite a number of years, I think that in the future we should make some provision for better control over our forces which may be detached for these special duties.

Cyprus Crisis
The Cyprus situation is in many respects even more difficult than the Congo operation and certainly much more than the Gaza strip. As the Leader of the Opposition pointed out on March 13 when he was discussing this subject, this operation really involves the intervention of a United Nations force in what is almost a civil war in Cyprus. That puts the United Nations forces in a somewhat different position from what they have been in before. The Leader of the Opposition, although approving of the dispatch of our troops, sounded a very proper note of warning with regard to this aspect because it is one thing to be a peace keeping force establishing a cordon sanitaire along the boundary between two nations and an entirely different thing to be a United Nations force right in the middle of a populace that is torn by internal troubles. There will be some effect, of course, on a government of a country that is having such internal troubles with a United Nations force within its borders.
The Cyprus operation is of such seriousness that I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) should reexamine the position of our Canadian troops there so that if we are involved in another similar operation we will be assured of better control over our forces. We might easily have very heavy casualties. It might happen through ineffective control within the United Nations forces. All of that would be unknown to us. We simply have to take it on faith that the United Nations force is going to be an effective military organization run on the best military lines. How do we know that will happen? I think we should be prepared to draw certain lessons from our activities in Cyprus and in other United Nations peace keeping operations.
I was interested in seeing in the Christian Science Monitor of August 4 last an article dealing with stand-by forces for the United Nations. In that article mention is made of the proposal of the Scandinavian states, Denmark, Norway and Sweden, to set up separate military forces to be kept in readiness for United Nations service. It is rather strange- I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs will take note of this-that there is no mention in that article in this very responsible and reputable newspaper of Canada's contribution in the way of stand-by forces for the United Nations.
