speechtext:
He discusses the way in which forces may be provided for the United Nations and I should like to draw attention to five statements of policy that he lays down. Briefly, the first one is that "the force shall assist only in peace keeping operations". The second is that "a lawfully adopted UN decision is required for the Scandinavian countries to make the earmarked forces available". We are familiar with that arrangement. The third is that "the country in which the forces are to be used shall have accepted the UN operation and our participation in it". In other words there must be an invitation from the country which requires assistance. I will deal with the fourth point later. The fifth is that "the force will be placed under the exclusive control of the United Nations". This is the

point I have just been questioning because of the lack of control by the nation that assigns its armed forces for this purpose. The fourth point is of very great interest in connection with what I have been saying and is put in these words:
UN requests can be complied with only after an independent appraisal of the general situation. This implies that the action proposed in the given circumstances must be acceptable to the governments of the Scandinavian countries. This may sound very restrictive and it does, in fact, imply a limitation. It means that the United Nations will not have the right automatically to draw on the Scandinavian stand-by force. But it should be borne in mind that in the final analysis it is a question of asking 4,000 young men to risk their lives for a cause which, being an international issue, affects their own countries only indirectly. A democratic government must make sure that the people understand and support its actions. That is why we have found it necessary to make this reservation.
In deciding whether a UN request should be complied with, all relevant circumstances-including national military security considerations-will be taken into account. As far as Denmark and Norway are concerned, we shall also bear in mind our obligations toward our allies.
But there can be no doubt that our basic attitude to any such requests will be a very positive one, in keeping with the general lines of our foreign policy in which support of the United Nations iorms a decisive element.
I think we would agree with most of that, but I do note the emphasis of the foreign minister of Denmark on the fact that their force, earmarked for use with the United Nations, might comprise 4,000 young men who would be asked to risk their lives for a cause, and that is what we are asking our young men to do when they are assigned to a United Nations force. There is a risk of life involved and I am concerned that completely adequate steps be taken before any such commitment is made, to ensure that their lives will not be uselessly endangered.
Coming back to what I said some time ago, that is why I am asking did the Secretary of State for External Affairs receive a military appraisal of the situation in Cyprus from the Minister of National Defence? Has he received a subsequent military appraisal of the situation from the minister? If not, from whence does he get his information as to the effectiveness of our force and its security? Who supplies the military appreciation? What does a battalion of infantry do under present circumstances, where war is perhaps imminent in that country? Is it able to provide adequate protection? If it is forced from one position to another, what is its base? Has it a base of operation at which it can defend
Cyprus Crisis
itself, and if necessary make a suitable withdrawal?
We hope none of this happens. We hope the peace keeping activities of the United Nations force in Cyprus will be effective. We hope a political settlement will be discovered by those conducting the negotiations, but all contingencies must be provided for, and this house is entitled to a precise statement from the Minister of National Defence or from the Secretary of State for External Affairs with regard to the safety of our troops. We have not had that yet and I hope the Minister of National Defence will give us the information tonight.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I consider that in the interests of world peace Canada has to continue to play its part in similar operations, which we call peace keeping operations. At the same time we must maintain our military strength in case it is required for war. We cannot simply train our forces for peace keeping operations alone. They must first be trained to fight. This other is in addition to their capabilities as fighting troops. I hope we do not lose sight of the fact that the purpose of national defence arrangements is to provide for the safety of one's own country. You sometimes provide for that safety by serving abroad. That is what our troops are doing in these far flung expeditions in various parts of the world.
We are naturally in support of activities of this nature, but I think it is only right that at times we should be a bit critical of the lack of information we have been getting. We have a right to examine the nature of our commitment and its cost, and we are certainly obliged to assure ourselves, in the interests of our country, that our troops are adequately prepared for any emergency and that their safety is not placed in jeopardy.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel every member of the house is grateful to the right hon. Leader of the Opposition for having moved this motion to adjourn the house to discuss this matter of such vital importance to Canadians and to the world as a whole. I commend the government and other parties in the house for having given unanimous consent to the debate. Unanimity in the house is such a rarity that it is really appreciated.
This debate has cleared the air. Those on the opposition side have expressed their opinions, and some were opinions of experts in military affairs. I propose to speak as an ordinary common man, and I for one appre-

Cyprus Crisis
ciate the minister giving us all the information he could. We share with him the feelings of emotion he had while giving us his report this afternoon. We commend him for carrying on his diplomatic activities in this delicate situation in such a way that Canada gave no appearance of taking sides in the struggle on Cyprus.
We are concerned, with him, as to what happens with these two links in the chain of NATO, that chain which has held back the communist invasion of Europe, which has saved democracy in Europe. A weakening of one link is important, but the weakening of two links would practically destroy NATO. Therefore we share the minister's concern that the chain remain strong and intact.
Canada answered the call first when the idea of a peace keeping force for Cyprus was propounded. One may wonder why. Was it to show off? Was it because we are so loyal to NATO and the United Nations, or was it because we were carried away by the successes we had in peace keeping operations in other parts of the world?
We were successful in the Congo, but we may have forgotten that the United Nations peace keeping force to the Congo went into a tribal area where the tribes were undisciplined, unarmed, and in many cases illiterate. We see now what is happening there after the United Nations forces have been removed. There is internal strife; war is in the offing, and there is another problem for the United Nations.
Canada participated successfully in the Gaza strip venture, and in other activities, and I think we were carried away when it came to the Cyprus operation. I think we deceived ourselves by the very fact that this flare-up was on a small island which has a population of 600,000. A force of 7,000 was organized, practically the same size as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who in Canada keep peace and order for almost 20 million people. It looked like a venture that was going to be harmless, and it seemed as though our boys would be back home in one or two months, at the outside three months, having seen a large part of the world and having done a good job.
According to present appearances, this is not so. I am not accusing the government. I am not accusing the Secretary of State for External Affairs or the Minister of National Defence. But I feel there was a duty upon them to have told this house that our boys were being sent to an island where 40,000 men had arms-whether they were actually

under arms, or possessed arms, is splitting hairs; I believe that by this time Premier Makarios has mobilized them and that there are 40,000 men under arms. I do not think any particular attention was paid to that. It was not stressed, anyway. I do not think any emphasis was placed on the fact that this so-called independent sovereign state of Cyprus, a member of the commonwealth, sovereign in every respect, had on its soil a contingent of 650 armed men from mainland Turkey, or that likewise there were 950 armed men there from Greece. I think if these things had been divulged and if proper emphasis had been placed upon them we might have understood that we were sending our boys, to use a memorable phrase from "The Charge of the Light Brigade", "into the mouth of hell" rather than on a holiday, or on a peace keeping mission. Worse than that, we were sending them with an authority less than some of our municipal police have in our municipalities out west.
Anyone-he does not have to be an expert in diplomacy, or military affairs, or international affairs, or any other affairs-could tell that Greece and Turkey, under the guise of sending replacements or under the guise of provisioning their respective contingents on the island, would be stirring up trouble, creating difficulties and encouraging their own compatriots to take whatever action they thought best. Probably the secretary general of the United Nations felt that by sending in this peace keeping force, small as it was, the Turkish and Greek Cypriots would be so impressed that they would be paralysed with fear.
I agree with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) that the force was a small one. I doubt whether in present circumstances increasing it tenfold would do any good. But I will come to that later. Anyway, the feeling was that the Cypriots, both Greek and Turkish, would be paralysed with fear. And probably they were for a brief period of time. But as weeks went by, this peace keeping force had to shuttle back and forth from point to point, putting out small conflagrations which kept arising between the Turkish and Greek Cypriots, incited no doubt by the contingents which were there from Greece and Turkey. In the meantime we learned from the press that Archbishop Makarios as prime minister had declared mobilization. So those 40,000 men who had arms were, no doubt, put under arms and are fully mobilized. And these men have had their training, if not in the immediate past, then in the past two or three

years, in their struggle for what they thought was independence. Then, fighting broke out between the Turkish and the Greek Cypriots. I believe it was a fight between the Turks and the Greeks. As a consequence, just a couple of days ago the Turkish air force bombarded the northwest portion of Cyprus creating havoc, destroying property and probably destroying some military posts while at the same time causing death, as well as injury to civilians both men and women to the extent that Premier Makarios was disturbed. Meanwhile, the United Nations peace keeping force, so we were told by the press and over the radio on Saturday night, particularly the Canadians, were packing their bags ready to sail home should the necessity arise.
Now this house is happy, and I think the whole nation is happy to have received a report over the press, television and radio, confirmed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that a cease fire has been established as a result of diplomatic efforts. I do not minimize the efforts of the hon. gentleman, his colleagues in the government and everyone else concerned, including the security council. But how long will this state of affairs last? Along with every other member of this house, I pray that it does last. But I venture to say it will only last if Turkey and Greece will it so-not Archbishop Makarios nor his vice-premier, because if anyone says that Archbishop Makarios is acting under constituted authority, he is wrong. According to the constitution, silly as it is, provision is made for one-fifth of the population to have a veto power, and whatever orders or proclamations the archbishop has made on behalf of the Cyprus government are without any legal status since they were not approved by the Turkish minority. I still say that this cease fire in Cyprus will last only as long as Greece and Turkey want it to last.
I think the security council, the great powers, the little powers and Canada itself should exert all the pressure they possibly can upon these two links in the NATO chain to hold to the terms of this cease fire and to assist the security council or the commission of 14 which drew up the constitution for this unhappy island to draw up a new constitution. The constitution which presently exists should be scrapped because, as I indicated, there is a most ridiculous provision in it whereby a minority has the power of veto. That is impossible. It would be impossible in this house and it is impossible in any nation. Second, I feel that the Secretary of
Cyprus Crisis
State for External Affairs should suggest to those who have greater influence over Greece and Turkey that these Greek and Turkish contingents should be removed from the island of Cyprus. This must happen if Cyprus is to remain a sovereign and independent state.
As long as they are stationed there, there is going to be no peace even, as I have said, if the peace keeping force there is increased. A new constitution should be drawn up. Far be it from us, at this distance and not knowing the conditions there, not knowing the historical background which it is necessary to know, to suggest the form of the constitution. But I have pointed out two ridiculous provisions, and I believe everyone in this house will agree with me that these two ridiculous provisions have led to the situation as it is on the island today.
The third thing that should be attempted is the disbanding of Makarios' army. That might be difficult, but the United Nations have had more difficult tasks. If the Turks do likewise, only then will 7,000 men of the United Nations peace keeping force be able to keep the peace. Without these changes, Mr. Speaker, as an ordinary man with no expert knowledge, I feel there will be no peace; at least, no permanent peace. Without these changes we must take steps to ask the United Nations to release our force and let the boys come back home, because they cannot serve any useful purpose. It is true that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said they have saved lives. I presume he means in connection with casualties suffered from the Turkish bombings and from flare-ups between the Turks and the Greeks. But that is not what the Canadian people understood was the purpose of sending this force there; we understood they were to be in the capacity of policemen-and if a police officer has no authority to intervene between two antagonists and use force if necessary to stop an unnecessary fight, his presence is absolutely useless.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is very little I can add to the very full report given the house by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) this afternoon. Nevertheless there are one or two points relating to the military aspects of the operation upon which I should like to comment briefly.
It is the responsibility of a military organization to anticipate to the fullest extent possible demands which may be made on its resources and to be prepared to meet those

Cyprus Crisis
demands. In accordance with, this responsibility the Department of National Defence anticipated that the rapidly deteriorating situation in Cyprus might require United Nations or other intervention involving a Canadian component. When this house took its decision on March 13 we were well prepared to act. That same day our advance party was dispatched to Cyprus, where it arrived the following day. Movement staffs and R.C.A.F. slip crews departed in two aircraft on March 14; troop airlift began the following day, March 15, and was completed on March 22; Her Majesty's Canadian ship Bonaventure departed Halifax March 18 and arrived at Famagusta March 30, carrying 95 personnel, 54 vehicles and 92 tons of cargo. The whole force was moved smoothly and quickly without incident, and its organization reflects great credit on our land, sea and air forces.
I might also say it was Canada's willingness and ability to send an advance party on March 13, together with the initiatives taken by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, which catalyzed the formation of the United Nations force, thereby removing the immediate threat of outbreak of hostilities existing at that time. The harmonious teamwork between the departments of external affairs and defence is a matter of gratification.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) has asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether or not he had at that time a military appreciation. The answer, Mr. Speaker, is of course he did. We were well aware of the facts as they existed at that time. We knew that almost every able-bodied Cypriot carried a rifle; we knew that it would be impossible for the small force envisaged by the United Nations to fight its way on to the island, and that it could only be useful if it went there in a peace keeping role with the active cooperation of the Cypriots themselves. It was on this basis that the force was formed. It was on the basis of the terms of reference which were agreed between the United Nations and the government of Cyprus that the force was formed and went forward.
In respect of the organization of the force, the command structure in Cyprus is organized into two zones and three districts. The zones are under Canadian and Swedish command. Two of the districts are under United Kingdom command and the third is under Finnish command. Headquarters, Nicosia zone, is commanded by Brigadier A. J. Tedlie, D.S.O., C.D., and the Canadian component on
[Mr. Hellyer.l
his staff consists of 19 officers and 137 other ranks. The Canadian contingent which serves in the Nicosia zone is commanded by E. A. C. Amy, D.S.O., O.B.E., M.C., C.D., and consists of the headquarters Canadian contingent, United Nations force in Cyprus; the 1st battalion of the Royal 22nd regiment, less one company; reconnaissance squadron, Royal Canadian Dragoons, and an administrative support group. The total strength of the contingent at June 29 was 82 officers and 1,021 other ranks. In addition, six officers and nine other ranks are employed at the headquarters of the United Nations force. The total strength of Canadians in Cyprus at June 29 was 88 officers and 1,030 other ranks. The force is supported by an R.C.A.F. flight each week from Canada. The job that has been done by the force and by the Canadian contingent in particular is, I think, little short of magnificent under the circumstances. I cannot praise it too highly.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
There have been many times when the force has avoided bloodshed. How many, I cannot say; but too many to catalogue. There have been many times when lives have been saved. There have been many times when the immediate and effective intervention of the force has prevented an outbreak of major violence. This is the reason the force was established and the reason it was sent there. It has, in addition, performed numerous other tasks. It has supervised the harvesting of the crops. Whether the harvest was for a Greek Cypriot community or a Turkish Cypriot community, in either event the force has accompanied the harvesters into the fields and supervised the taking of the crops. This has been a very valuable service to the island and to both communities there.
In addition, the force has been able to restore a certain degree of normalcy in some areas. Arrangements have been made to permit the flow of citizens from one community through the lines of the other in order to perform certain useful work. All these very important tasks are in accord with the mandate that was given the force at the time it was established and sent there to do its work. I may say that the young men of our contingent are excellent ambassadors for Canada. I do not know when I have been so impressed with a body of men, young soldiers of 18, 19, 20, 21 years of age showing the maturity and common sense and

good judgment which you would expect from people much older in years.
One of the incidents which I should like to relate-and this is true-is this. One of our deployments in a most difficult area is directly between the outposts of the two Greek and Turkish communities. Periodically firing would commence between the two outposts, and a young corporal 21 years of age would pick up the phone and say: "Now, you cut that out". And they did. It may be a strange kind of war, but I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that our young men have been very effective and you would be most proud of them if you had the opportunity to see them operating as effectively as they do under these very difficult circumstances.

speechtext: You had better send that boy home. We could use him in this house.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Yes. It is just not true to say, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) said in the House of Commons this afternoon, that the force is as helpless as if it were non-existent. The powers given the force may be too limited, but they were the best which could be arranged. I think this is essentially a thing for us to remember, that had there been no agreement there would have been no force, and the bloodshed would have continued. The agreement which was reached was the best which could be determined at the time the force was set up.
The deployment of the forces in Cyprus, however, is a peace keeping deployment, not a military deployment, and it depends for its effectiveness on the active co-operation of the local authorities. More recently violations of the status quo have made the situation much more difficult. In these circumstances Canada has taken every possible initiative. I should like to take this opportunity to pay a well deserved tribute to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin). No one has worked more assiduously, shown more initiative or put more effort into the determination of a reconciliation of the situation in that troubled island than my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He has been untiring in what he has done, and I should like to say to my hon. friend from Winnipeg South, or South Centre-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Your friend is Winnipeg South; I am your enemy.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I would say to my hon. friend for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) that in respect to supervision of ports, in that case too the Secretary of State for External
Cyprus Crisis
Affairs has taken the matter up with the United Nations. He did not neglect to do his duty in that regard. Anyone who knows the Secretary of State for External Affairs well, as I do, knows that he would have done it, and I quote, "with the sternest of admonitions". Notwithstanding the best efforts the problem is still not yet solved. Meanwhile, the usefulness of the United Nations force remains while further effort is made to effect a settlement.
The hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) suggested that a consultative or advisory committee, including the representatives of contributing countries and of Greece, Turkey and Cyprus, might be helpful in advising the secretary general on the problems faced by the United Nations force. He recalled that a similar committee had been established for the United Nations force in the Congo.
I think these points might be put on the record. When the United Nations force in Cyprus was established the United Nations secretary general considered that, initially at least, he would wish to consult individually with contributing countries and with the parties directly concerned, and he has been regularly following this practice. Second, the situation facing the United Nations in Cyprus is different in important respects from that which faced the organization in the Congo. A procedure which is suitable for an operation in one country does not always work for an operation in another. In Cyprus there are special circumstances which make the UN operation particularly delicate, and an advisory committee therefore, with the membership suggested by the hon. member for Oxford, would probably be less flexible and satisfactory than the secretary general's present policy of consulting countries individually. Consultations on a future settlement for Cyprus with the leaders of the two communities and the Greek and Turkish governments have, of course, been carried out by the UN mediator in accordance with the March 4 resolution of the security council.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) has raised the question as to the position of Canadian troops in the event of another serious crisis. He argues, and I agree, that the Canadian people are entitled to some assurance that our forces will not be put in an indefensible position. His concern is shared by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) and others.
In order to allay fears I should like to say something about our contingency plan. I am sure hon. members appreciate the delicacy of

Cyprus Crisis
the subject. The United Nations force, including our contingent, was sent to Cyprus-and I quote from part of the security council resolution of March 4-"in the interests of preserving international peace and security, to use its best efforts to prevent a recurrence of fighting and as necessary to contribute to the maintenance and restoration of law and order". It is therefore not consistent with the purposes to which the force was formed to talk about withdrawal.
However, from a directly military point of view those directly responsible for the security of our forces would be remiss in their duty if they did not give adequate forethought to the effects of a possible emergency. In this connection it was appreciated from the outset that a solution to the Cyprus situation would not be easy. It was also appreciated that under certain circumstances a situation might arise which would make it impossible for the force to perform a useful function. I therefore asked the chief of staff to prepare a plan which could be capable of implementation in the event of a crisis. This was for some considerable length of time a very well kept secret. In June I discussed the situation with our commander in Cyprus and as a result certain modifications were worked out designed to increase the effectiveness of the plan and to correlate it with the situation as applied to the whole United Nations force. I am satisfied that sufficient provision has been made to cope with any situation which is likely to arise. For obvious reasons it would be unwise to give details of contingency plans.
However on one rather important point I should like to reassure the hon. member for Calgary North. Whereas some of our troops are deployed in peace keeping positions in the Kyrenia area, authority has been delegated to the UN commander to alter the deployment and regroup the force in company positions if developing circumstances should warrant such action. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) told the house, "the situation in Cyprus is difficult; we knew that before we sent our troops there on March 13".
Two points should be made perfectly clear. First, there is no intention of withdrawing our contingent of United Nations force from Cyprus. Second, should an emergency arise, however, which would make the continued operation of the force impractical, adequate plans are available to cope with that kind of situation.

I should like to reiterate the belief that there remains an essential task to be performed. Notwithstanding events of the last few days there is still hope that a settlement may be reached. Negotiations continue at Geneva and there has been a disposition to work toward a solution.
It may well be that some change in the authority of the United Nations force will be required if a settlement is to be applied. General Thimayya, as hon. gentlemen know, is reporting to the secretary general tonight, and I believe that his report is to be discussed at a security council meeting tomorrow. He may indeed have some suggestions in this regard. There have been changes in directives from time to time and there may be further changes in the future. When I returned from Cyprus I expressed the opinion that broader powers might be required if a solution was imposed. Nothing that has happened in the meantime has changed my view.
First, however, a solution must be agreed which will have the support of the powers involved. Once that has been done, if it can be, the role of the United Nations force in the application of the settlement will be selfapparent. It would not be feasible, I am sure, for national governments to retain day to day control of their forces as suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill). With his extensive military experience I am sure he will be the first to realize that it would be chaotic and utterly impossible if the force commander was required to consult each member government in advance of each move.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped the minister's remarks would make it unnecessary for me to speak, but there are certain points he did not cover, and others I think he has glossed over. I therefore, hope with some brief remarks to dispose of some of the questions that remain unanswered.
The situation today, five months after the initial debate which led to the resolution for Canada to offer its forces to the United Nations, if it was not overshadowed by the tragedy of hundreds of innocent lives lost during the attacks of this week end, does provide us with an opportunity of reviewing that which has happened in respect of this Cyprus force. I think everyone will agree that this force was created by way of an experiment. The United Nations is still feeling its way in this regard. There is no set type of peace keeping operation. This is a unique situation in that there was an invitation on the part of the government of Cyprus rather than forces outside it being involved initially. There was no aggression from a force outside of Cyprus. The whole operation is being carried out in an attempt to keep down an insipient civil war between intercommunal forces within the country.
We know difficulties exist within the framework of security forces. There is always a grave difficulty in respect of international bodies in that they tend to become top heavy. Each party feels it should have the appropriate number of majors, colonels and brigadiers. This involves the old business of a lot of chiefs and not too many Indians. Such a body becomes somewhat unwieldy. As a result of the information I have received in respect of Cyprus I rather suspect that such is the case there. It has been the case in other areas, including the Congo and the Middle East. This is a difficulty inherent to this type of operation. We must learn a lesson in this respect from the Cyprus situation, and attempt to work out this rather top heavy structure.
We must be sure we have capable field commanders, and that is not always the case. I thought the minister was rather naive when he indicated we committed our Canadian troops with the knowledge that we had a competent field commander. If my memory serves me correctly parliament did not know who was going to be the United Nations force commander at the time this resolution was before us.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I just point out to my hon. friend that the night before the force was established I was told who the commander would be, if the force was established.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The minister now tells me that immediately prior to the decision by this house to establish such a force he knew the identity of the field commander; but that is not always the case. I rather think that under the circumstances it was a little odd, in that if Canada had not taken the initiative there would not have been field forces, and how then could you have had a commander? Perhaps a name had been suggested. In any event, I will leave that point.
I am also concerned about the nature and quality of the troops sent to do this job. Frankly, are the troops properly trained for the job they are to do? We take our most battle trained unit, supposedly our most highly honed unit and send it off, not to do battle but on a peace keeping mission, really a police or provost type of job. My colleague from Ontario says that the minister emphasized that these troops have overseen the harvesting of the crops.
I am not detracting at all from the unit that was sent but I am wondering whether under the circumstances it was the best unit to send. If another emergency had arisen meanwhile where we had needed a battle trained unit, our best one was already committed. The minister knew ahead of time what the role of our forces was going to be and what was going to be permitted, so why send these particular troops?
I raise that question because I feel that a different type of troops could be sent to do this type of job. We have spoken of the difficulties, and this afternoon the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) indicated that he was somewhat concerned and uneasy about the terms of reference finding them rather limiting. I am sure the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) feels even more concerned about them because I am certain that the sense of frustration of our Canadian troops in Cyprus has been communicated to him. If it has not, then I certainly am aware of it because for seven weeks now our troops have known that both the Greeks and the Turks have been sin


reptitiously beefing up their forces by slipping in regularly trained troops, and our troops have been powerless to stop it. This is the Achilles heel of the whole operation.
It is all very well to supervise thq harvesting of crops and other rather more peaceful activities. However, when the purpose is to keep the peace and you can see potential enemies arming and are powerless to stop it, surely to goodness it can be realized just how frustrating the job is. Let me give the minister an example of frustration. The house will excuse me for making a personal reference. In 1945 I was a prisoner of war in a camp that had an assortment of some 50,000 officers, air force and army, United States, British, South African, Australian and what have you. When liberation came the German camp authorities fled and the American troops that had liberated the camp went on as they were fighting an S.S. division. Immediately there was an exodus from the camp. People scrounged wire cutters from field troops. Others just climbed the wire and over they went with, I suppose, a feeling of freedom. They were a great nuisance to the field commanders and unfortunately there were some regrettable incidents.
There were some U.S.S.R. troops and others who were feeling a little dry, I suppose, and they got hold of some local spirits. Frankly, the situation got rather chaotic until the American force commander indicated to the camp seniors that everybody would have to remain inside the camp or else we would be faced with the rather unseemly prospect of American military police being stationed in the guard boxes to guard allied, including American, officers and keep them within the compound.
So a camp guard was organized and it was the lot of the junior officers to man the guard 24 hours a day. At that time I was a lieutenant and therefore it became my lot on two occasions to man the guard. There were always people wanting to get beyond the wire. They still had wire cutters. They would cut the wire and get out. There were also people on the outside trying to get in. Certainly the group of Soviet prisoners of war was of some concern to us because they had got hold of arms. We did not have arms and the Russians would return at all hours rather inebriated and we did not know what they were going to do. I remember how frustrated and useless I felt, as did almost all of those who were perimeter guards, because of the orders we were given. Those orders were to this effect: Officers on guard duty will not be armed. In

the event that personnel attempt to get out of camp or to come into camp they will be dissuaded from doing so by the guard officers using their personalities. At two o'clock in the morning, Mr. Speaker, in a mist next to a water filled ditch you are glad, when four or five Soviet troops approach you with rifles, that they are just happy and not belligerent because just your personality is of little use against a rifle.
This was the feeling of frustration we had and this is the feeling of frustration that the United Nations troops, not only the Canadians, have in Cyprus. I would have had a lot to say about the bona fides of the Cypriot government. Since it could not keep the peace itself and agreed to the entry of United Nations forces I would have thought that the least one could expect was that it would act in a bona fide way; but such is not the case. We simply have to read the editorial in this morning's Gazette in which the following statement attributed to Archbishop Makarios is quoted:
Where requirements of absolute security on matters of state defence and security are involved, it is not possible to permit entry of UN patrols.
What utter nonsense to have to face such a stand. This is the biggest possible umbrella for all sorts of clandestine activities, and that is precisely what is being done. There has not been the necessary bona fides on the part of the Cypriot government. In so far as the other two governments, Greece and Turkey, are concerned, naturally they have fallen short of the bona fides that we would have liked in this matter because both sides did bring in troops. I have seen reports that President Makarios has 15,000 trained troops under arms. They were not bringing lollipops ashore from the convoys that were reported. These men are prepared. Certainly no one in the house would advocate the withdrawal of the Canadian troops under the present circumstances. This would spell the death knell of United Nations peace keeping forces and the whole philosophy of such efforts. But surely to goodness we now see what has been done under the arrangements that have existed for the past five months.
What is necessary? If they wish to avoid war the members of the United Nations must see to the strengthening of the United Nations forces. There we have another problem. Here in Canada we have concluded a three month period. We are now almost at the end of the second three month period, all at Canada's cost. We are not complaining about that, but
Cyprus Crisis
how long is this going to last? It is quite conceivable that this might last for a year or 18 months.
If we are to strengthen the forces, at whose expense will this be done? Is this going to be a regularly constituted force under the United Nations? The United Nations has just had a very sobering experience in the Congo. It may be that the nations of the world love to pay lipservice to peace, but are not prepared to pay the shot. I believe the sincerity of their desire for world peace is measured precisely by their performance. Unfortunately some have been woefully weak. Some have gone to the other end of the pendulum by refusing to pay.
Canada, as well as the others involved in this particular peace keeping enterprise, must press for an extension of the terms of reference. It must press not only directly through the United Nations upon Archbishop Makarios, but through its allies so that we may mount an offensive of public opinion on Archbishop Makarios whereby he can have no alternative but to agree that the appropriate terms of reference for a strong peace keeping effort be made available to the United Nations troops. In my opinion this is where we must concentrate our efforts, and perhaps the tragic events of this last week end will help to mount this offensive of public opinion so that President Makarios will have to accept these forces not on the terms-well, I could go into similes but they might be thought to be slanderous, so I will not go into them.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, there are still some unresolved questions. We may have been starry eyed five months ago when we were rushing blithely off like a knight errant in shining armour but we have now had one or two tumbles into wayside puddles. The armour is no longer so shiny and we know the road is long and rough.
I hope we can give encouragement to our troops by getting them an extension of their terms of reference, certainly to disarm and to watch the ports so that this stockpiling of arms will be discontinued. I just cannot conceive of any peace keeping or police type of activity where, if you discover people with clandestine arms you leave them in their possession, one where you do nothing at all unless they fire at you and then you fire back. But you do not take away their arms. This is certainly the height of unreality and I hope we can get our troops out of this rather unsatisfactory position.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) has stated that an appreciation was made of this situation in Cyprus before troops were committed, and has been done again since then. I take it that all the factors have been studied, that as a result we have perceived an intention in our objective, and that we know precisely from a military point of view how we are going to carry out that intention.
From what the minister has said, I disagree that our appreciation has been complete; but before going into that matter may I say Canada has always been ready, willing and able at all times, during war and also in her peace keeping activities through the United Nations. We have had many men of ability who have proved themselves to a very great extent indeed, but that has always been when the role or object is known, and known in detail. All down the line we Canadians have had a great deal of pride in all phases of our military forces, and with justification; but this is a little different.
The situation in Cyprus at the moment is not out of hand but it is extremely volatile. It is a situation which could break into a war, however limited, and no doubt tonight all over Canada wives, children and relatives are wondering to what extent the Canadian forces are committed. They cannot help but wonder because their boys are over there on a mission, and that mission, so we understand, is a police force of sorts, peace keeping in essence.
When, then, does that role change, or when might it change? This is where I differ from the Minister of National Defence. Frankly I think he was running off at the mouth at times; he was merely saying a whole bunch of words, because he said if things get a little difficult we will come back to Canada and find out here what is to be done. What I want to impress upon the minister is the volatile nature of the situation over there, and what might happen when Canadians, among others forming that peace keeping force, may be involved over and above their peace keeping role. To my mind this is of tremendous importance.
If the minister thinks that if trouble breaks out he can then come back to Canada and say, "What are we going to do?" I can tell him he is going to be too late altogether. I want to know, and I hope some Liberals want to know, what is Canada's role and how far we are implicated if trouble breaks out? If trouble breaks out can our commander on the 
spot take certain definite steps or must he ask one of two things-what does the United Nations say to do, or what does my country say to do?
In making his little speech tonight the minister said that if the commander disagrees with the role given to him at a time of stress, and under duress, he can then come back to Canada. Holy Christmas. Does the minister not understand that when a war is on you do not have time to do these things? The minister shakes his head to indicate he did not say that, but I can correct Hansard as well as he can and I know exactly what he said because I jotted it down at the time. If the role appears too difficult, the commander can come back to Canada. What utter balderdash.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: You are right. I did not say it. You did.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The minister says he did not say it. Already he is backtracking. Let me say to him, despite the laughter from the Liberal benches, that Canadian troops are over there under fire and subject to being killed at the present time, and if this situation gets a little worse, what are those troops under the Canadian commander going to do? The minister did say he could raise the matter with Canada. I tell the minister that time in a volatile situation does not permit reference to anyone. Canadians may be involved. We have asked questions repeatedly in this house for the last number of months. We have addressed them to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of National Defence. Always the answer has been: Look, this subject is a little touchy; we cannot answer it.
What will happen if war breaks out over there? May I finish with one question? Suppose Canada, under United Nations command, does reply in kind, in self-defence, and people are killed when shots are fired; precisely what is Canada's position? Is Canada involved in a war? What are the United Nations instructions in this regard?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Before we proceed to the orders of the day I wish to take the time of the house for a few minutes, largely because of a message which has come in and which I should like to place on record.
Before I do that, may I express my appreciation of the initiative of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) in bringing about this discussion on such an important subject, and of the level on which the dis-

cussion has been conducted. We have learned, I think, through this debate that there are members on the other side who certainly appreciate and understand the difficulties and the dangers we are facing in our participation in United Nations activities of this kind. It was said by one hon. member that last March we, and the government, may have entered upon this undertaking in a spirit of knight errantry and easy idealism without awareness of its dangers. Mr. Speaker, anyone who has had anything to do with international peace keeping operations at any time in the last 10 or 15 years is not likely to enter into an undertaking such as the Cyprus undertaking without an awareness of the danger and difficulties, let alone in any spirit of knight errantry. There is nothing more complicated or more difficult than operations of this kind, as we learned in the Suez crisis and as some of the hon. gentlemen opposite learned when they led Canadian participation in the Congo operation. Now there is the Cyprus operation which is, in some respects, the most difficult of all.
An understanding of these difficulties is certainly widespread in the house. Similarly, we on this side of the house share the feelings of impatience and, at times, of frustration which anyone must feel at the inability of an international force to achieve clear cut objectives in a way which is so often laid down when an undertaking is a national one. But we also know, with the responsibility of government, that it is not possible to achieve perfection in a matter of this kind. As the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said, we are feeling our way; we are groping; we are going from stage to stage and we are trying, on the foundation we have laid, to build up a structure of peace keeping. It cannot be an easy or a quick undertaking and there are things we would have liked to see done in connection with the terms of reference, the directives, the operations and the authority given to the force, but which could not be done because of the necessity of reaching agreement with the United Nations, with the other governments concerned, and particularly with the government of the country in which the force has to operate.
Back in 1956 when we were trying to work out the terms of reference and orders for the United Nations emergency force in the Suez, we soon found that in order to operate in the area we had to achieve co-operation with the government, or the leader of the government, in the territory in which the force would operate. You cannot have clear cut objec-20220-419	.
Cyprus Crisis
tives and clearcut authority, because there has to be compromise. When the Congo force was set up its terms of reference were very much like those which govern the operations of the United Nations force in Cyprus-they were to use force only in self-defence, as is the case in Cyprus. But as the months went by it became clear that there had to be changes in the directive. Changes were made, but it took a good many months to bring them about and it was not done until conditions in the Congo made it essential that changes should be made. And there may have to be changes in connection with United Nations activities in Cyprus, and the crisis through which we have gone this week end may make the necessity for these changes more obvious to certain people than has been the case up to this moment. Sometimes you can do things under the impetus of fear that you cannot do under the stimulus of reason. So perhaps out of the crisis of the week end, if we can get through it without too much trouble-and things look a little better, now-we may be able to strengthen the position of the United Nations force in Cyprus.
Certainly this crisis has shown one thing clearly. It has shown that the United Nations, with all its weakness and imperfection, is indispensable in keeping the peace at times of crisis as well as between crises in a situation of this kind. If the United Nations had not moved in last March we might have been in a desperate situation in the eastern Mediterranean, and who knows how far the conflict might have extended? If the United Nations and the security council in particular had not been available over the week end, we do not know what might have happened. But it was there. It was able to take up the situation on Friday and Saturday and at least bring about a cease fire. This does not end the dispute, of course, but it has given us another chance to bring about an agreement and I hope the members of the United Nations will be able to take advantage of the opportunity which has now been afforded to them. The situation has eased, but the problem is not solved.
A message just came in which confirms the easing of the situation. It is a statement made by the secretary general on the Cyprus situation, and perhaps before we reach orders of the day I might be permitted to place it on the record. This is what U Thant has to say this evening:
The president of the security council on 9 August, pursuant to the wishes of the council, directed urgent appeals to the governments of Cyprus and Turkey to end their hostile activities by a cease-

Cyprus Crisis
fire. It is gratifying and encouraging that both governments have responded positively and without conditions. On the morning of 10 August the president of Cyprus informed the president of the security council by cable that "We shall respect the appeal of the security council for a cease-fire''; and addressed a similar cable to me.
That is, the secretary general;
In a letter to the president of the security council, received on the afternoon of the same day, the prime minister of Turkey stated that the government of Turkey "Has decided to stop immediately the action of the Turkish aircraft over the Mansoura-Kokkina region-"
The secretary general goes on;
"These decisions of the two governments now afford an opportunity for definitely ending fighting and relaxing tension in Cyprus, and it will be my purpose to take fullest possible advantage of this opportunity by exerting every effort toward constructive peace keeping arrangements in all areas of the island. In consequence, I have instructed the commander of the force to co-operate fully with all parties in making the cease-fire thoroughly effective and to take every initiative and to lend all assistance toward this end. I strongly appeal to the governments of Cyprus, Greece and Turkey and to the Turkish community of Cyprus to extend full co-operation and support to General Thimayya and to the United Nations force in Cyprus which he commands in their peace keeping efforts.
"I have also asked Mr. Galo Plaza, my special representative in Cyprus, to return there promptly and it is expected that he will do so by the end of the week."
This is encouraging as far as it goes. I know, from the discussion that has taken place today, that all members of the house will back the government, speaking for Canada, in this matter and in its endeavours to support the secretary general and the United Nations in all the efforts that can be made, not only to resolve this particular crisis but to bring a solution of the problem in Cyprus.
We in this country certainly have an interest in that island. We have an interest because Cyprus is a sister nation in the commonwealth of nations, and it might have been possible in other circumstances for the commonwealth to have done something to restore peace to that island, except that the two countries outside Cyprus most directly affected are not members of the commonwealth. We have an interest in this crisis as members of NATO, and it might have been possible in different circumstances for NATO to have intervened positively and constructively in this matter, except that the country most directly concerned, Cyprus, is not a member of NATO, and NATO intervention in the circumstances which existed might not have been the most effective way of removing suspicions and bringing about peace. We are

a member of the United Nations, and that is the source of our own participation in this operation.
Mr. Speaker, if this operation does not succeed, if this crisis had deteriorated into conflict-which I hope and believe now it will not-it would have been the end of NATO. It might also have been the end of the peace keeping activities and endeavours of the United Nations, which are beginning to show more signs of progress than we had any right to expect a year or two ago. So from every point of view this crisis over the week end was more than a crisis of peace or war in Cyprus; it was concerned with the building up of international security in the world. We in Canada have from the beginning of the United Nations played our full part in that effort, and we will continue to do so.
We had an even deeper interest than this. We had an interest in this crisis because, as my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I think it was, said this afternoon, we belong to the human race and a conflict in a small part of the world, in a small island in the Mediterranean, involving only a few hundred thousand people can, through the awful escalation of modern political and military activities, develop into global nuclear warfare. If that happens, then indeed we will find out whether we are going to belong to the human race very much longer. So from every point of view, as a member of NATO, as a member of the commonwealth, as a member of the United Nations and as a member of the human race, I think we in this house would all want to do anything we can to bring about peace and security in this Mediterrean island.

CONGO; VIET NAM-SAFETY OF CANADIANS
On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs. It seems that we cannot leave him alone, but unfortunately there are critical international situations in other parts of the world as well. There are the situations in Viet Nam and in the Congo, which affect the safety and well-being of many Canadian nationals in those areas. Can the minister give us the assurance that our Canadian nationals in both these areas are being adequately taken care of?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have nothing further to add to what I said on Friday about the situation in the Congo. I had reference at that time to a particular family, and our reports are that they have not come to any harm.
With regard to the situation in Viet Nam, as my hon. friend knows, since the events toward the end of last week there have been no further major incidents. From the notice of the question my hon. friend gave me, I think he wanted me to give an indication of the number of Canadians in Viet Nam. There are 12 members of the Department of External Affairs and 54 members of the Canadian armed forces in Viet Nam. maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after spending the whole day on the rather important, and to some of us rather obscure, problems in international affairs I rather hesitate to bring the committee of the whole house back to the question of domestic arrangements.
Several members of the committee who have already spoken on this item, or who spoke on second reading of the bill, pointed out the importance of equalization payments from a central government to various provincial governments in a federal state. It should be obvious, and I think it is to almost everyone, that this is necessary because in a federal state the economic pattern of the various parts making up that state is varied in ways that are very difficult to measure or even estimate. For example, the imposition of tariffs may have a different effect on one province than on another, yet all provinces, of course, submit to the turning over of this power to the central government for the common good.
Tariffs may tend to create a concentration of manufacturing in one part of the country. That has taken place in Canada. I hope, however, that the tendency which has existed since confederation until practically the present time for concentration of manufacturing in central Canada will be reversed and there will be perhaps not an actual dispersion of manufacturing but an increase in the number of manufacturing interests in the various provinces so there will be more equity and an opportunity of employment resulting from this development.
When you have a concentration of manufacturing in one area you naturally have a concentration of other businesses in these areas. I will cite one example. In my province I think it is almost impossible, if not impossible, to buy life insurance without the knowledge that the premium paid each year probably goes to Montreal, Toronto, Waterloo or one of the insurance centres of the country. I do not cite this example because I have an objection to this fact but to show that this does create a concentration of the management and wealth as well as the management and investment capital in certain areas and it is more likely to be invested in these areas than in the extremities of the country. There are an infinite number of other examples that one might cite.
Various members who have spoken in this debate have pointed out the necessity and good sense of equalization payments. I think the minister summed this up perhaps as well


as anyone, and I hope he does not object if I put on the record again what he said in this connection as reported on page 5182 of Hansard for July 7, 1964:
If the equalization system is inadequate, the poorer provinces will be unduly burdened in their attempt to maintain reasonable standards in the public services for which they are responsible; and if they fail to maintain a reasonable standard of essential services, the national interest is affected.
Having said that, I should add that the argument for the equalization of the standard taxes to the level of the top two provinces does not rest on grounds of fairness or broad national interest alone. The provincial origins of the incomes and accumulations of wealth upon which income tax and estate tax yields depend are often widespread and are rarely known with accuracy. This in itself would, I suggest, support the view that some portion of their yield ought to be equalized among the various provinces.
Mr. Chairman, I thoroughly agree with that sentiment, but would like to concern myself with the actions of the government and the minister in this regard as well as with their words. Before doing so I should like to state that there is another factor rarely brought to light, and that is that many of the provinces in the extremities of the country make a great indirect contribution to the national good because they form markets for much of the manufactured goods manufactured in central Canada. The converse is not true to the same extent. This is especially true of provinces such as Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland where imports, to use the word in the provincial sense, of practically all manufactured goods come from central Canada. Most of our exports are exported entirely out of the country, and I refer to fish, minerals and pulp and paper products. This tendency is true of Prince Edward Island, but perhaps to a lesser extent.
The commercial activities of these provinces make great contributions to the balance of our import and export account, and help to reduce an otherwise great problem in respect of the balance of payments, with which we are always struggling.
Professor James M. Buchanan of the University of Virginia in an article on "Federalism and Fiscal Equity" published in the September, 1950 issue of the American Economic Review had this to say:
The (equity) principle establishes a firm basis for the claim that the citizens of the low income states within a national economy possess the "right" that their states receive sums sufficient to enable these citizens to be placed in positions of fiscal equality with their equals in other states. A transfer viewed in this light is in no sense a gift or subsidy from the citizens of the more favoured regions.

That is a principle that is very sound indeed, and although it is made in the context of the United States, I feel it applies with equal force to Canada.
I am concerned, as is the government of Prince Edward Island, with the present situation in respect of that province. In other words, I am concerned with the results of the two recent provincial conferences. I think the minister knows that the government of Prince Edward Island was bitterly disappointed with the results. That is not to say there is not some advantage gained. There was some considerable advantage gained from the new additional grants. However, they are not as great relatively as was generally hoped.
I should like to quote briefly, if I may, from the brief which the premier of Prince Edward Island presented to the federal-provincial conference in this connection. He stated:
The province of Prince Edward Island is claiming the recognition of a right-the principle of fiscal equality. A return for the money our people are paying each year in the form of higher prices, due to the tariffs, etc. which have had the effect of protecting manufacturing in central Canada. This protection has contributed greatly to the continued industrial expansion in that area that brought with it a concentration of income and wealth that is earned in doing business with all parts of the country.
We are not asking for any privilege. We do not want any privilege. We are anxious to co-operate with the other provinces and with the federal authorities in examining and exploring our mutual problems and presenting our views on matters of great concern.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISION
speechtext: I wonder whether I might ask the hon. gentleman a question. Is he aware that of the total amount of additional revenues that will be transferred or abated to the provinces for the fiscal year 1966-67 Prince Edward Island will receive $1,621,000? I have not worked it out on a per capita basis but it is certainly pretty high.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISION
speechtext:
I have worked it out and I am coming to that in just a moment. This is the nub of my argument. I might say in this connection that among the provinces Prince Edward Island in particular has exploited about as far it can in any reasonable way its own sources of taxation, because when you have a situation where the average income is lower than in other parts of the country you have a lesser tax base and the returns are bound to be less.
If I may take one field of provincial taxation as an example, let us consider the tax on gasoline. In Prince Edward Island it is
Federal-Provincial Relations 18 cents a gallon. There are only two other provinces with a gasoline tax higher, namely Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. The other provinces have a gasoline tax as low as 12 or 13 cents in many cases. As a matter of fact, west of Ontario 14 cents a gallon is the highest provincial tax on gasoline.
I should like to illustrate this point further by showing that the abatement of the income tax or the opportunity of provinces that have a low average income to collect certain taxes is not of very great benefit to them. I cite one example which illustrates the unequal tax capacities of the provinces. A 10 per cent increase in personal income tax in Prince Edward Island would yield about 30 cents per capita compared with $1.50 per capita in Ontario. So there is a real problem in this connection.
The problem is aggravated by the fact that the basic economy of Prince Edward Island is founded on the agricultural industry and the fishing industry and both of these industries are low income industries in relation to most other industries in Canada. Per capita income is also lowered by the fact that the percentage of wage earners in Prince Edward Island is smaller than in other provinces. This is due to the fact that there is insufficient opportunity in the maritime provinces generally for young people. I am not blaming this government for that because the situation has existed for many years. A great number of our young people who come into the labour market are forced to go to other provinces to earn their living. This leaves an inordinately high percentage of old people and children. I do not have the statistics but I am quite sure that in Prince Edward Island the percentage of dependants to wage earners is for this reason higher than in any other province of Canada.
The situation which exists in the maritimes creates added burdens for the governments there because they must provide educational facilities, to cite only one example, for the young people who are growing up and who as soon as they finish their education, which is provided to them by the provincial government at very considerable expense, go somewhere else. They have to do so because of economic conditions and they are presented, as it were, as a gift to some other province. A young man or young lady fully educated at the expense of one province goes to another province where economic opportunities are greater and adds in every way to the welfare of the latter province by becoming a taxpayer

Federal-Provincial Relations there during the period of life when they are
most productive.
I will try to finish before 10.30, Mr. Chairman, but I will not guarantee it. The minister has referred to the seemingly large amount of money, $1,621,000 additional a year, that Prince Edward Island will receive by 1966-67. This is .6 per cent of the total increment which will be paid to all the provinces in that year. The population of Prince Edward Island is roughly .52 per cent of the total population of Canada so the province is just a little slice better off than if it had been done on a flat per capita basis right across the country.
To take other figures I would point out that for the year 1962-63 Prince Edward Island received .79 per cent of the total amount. I have forgotten what the exact amount is in the case of Prince Edward Island but it does not matter. In the year 1964-65 it will receive .63 per cent of the increment. In the year 1965-66 it will receive .61 per cent of the increment and in the year 1966-67 it will receive .60 of the increment. In all cases its percentage of the increment is less than what its percentage of the total formerly was.
I am not complaining about the fact that there is going to be an extra $1,621,000 for Prince Edward Island but I am complaining about the fact that every year Prince Edward Island is receiving a relatively smaller slice of the pie. No matter how you work it out, Prince Edward Island is not doing as well
on the division of the increment as it formerly did from the grants which were worked out by all the governments in the past and culminated in the total grants that were given to the various provinces in 1962-63. This is the point about which we complain.
I am also rather curious about the wide variation in the total amounts given to the provinces. For example, although Prince Edward Island by 1966-67 will receive this amount New Brunswick will receive over $11 million more and Quebec $107 million more. These provinces are not that many times larger than Prince Edward Island and relatively I do not think their problems are as great.
May I call it 10.30, Mr. Chairman.
Progress reported.
